cleanTMLE: An R Package for Staged, Outcome-Blind Targeted Learning with Plasmode Data-Quality Stress Testing

Author
Affiliation

Andrew Mertens

University of California, Berkeley

Published

September 19, 2026

Abstract

Two failures poison comparative analyses of real-world data. The first is analyst degrees of freedom: when the person choosing the model can see how each choice moves the answer, the final estimate carries those peeks, however honest the person. The second is quieter and worse. Some comparisons are not estimable at all, and the estimator does not say so. An average treatment effect requires every kind of patient to have had a real chance of receiving either treatment; when a whole stratum essentially never receives one of them, the estimator extrapolates rather than refusing, and truncation limits its variance without touching the extrapolation. The result can be an estimate that is wrong by an order of magnitude inside a narrow confidence interval. A clean-room design (Muntner et al. 2024) addresses the first failure by fixing the design before anyone sees the treatment-outcome association. It does nothing about the second: a perfectly blinded team can still promise an estimand the data cannot deliver.

cleanTMLE is an R package that answers the estimability question during the blind phase of a staged analysis of a binary point-treatment study, and then estimates with targeted maximum likelihood. The design stage grades the overlap on the fitted propensity score, reads the same fit per estimand (the effect among the treated and the overlap-weighted effect can remain estimable where the average treatment effect is not), profiles the patients a trimmed analysis would no longer be about, and maps, with an outcome-blind plasmode simulation over a prespecified family of outcome surfaces, where each estimand’s estimator stays within a bias tolerance at near-nominal coverage. A pre-registered estimand ladder then makes switching to a feasible fallback a logged design decision rather than a silent substitution. The simulation uses the generate-treatment plasmode design throughout; keeping each subject’s observed treatment, the common alternative, induces a positivity violation by construction (Shaw et al. 2025). The package extends the same loop with a plasmode data-quality stress test that evaluates each candidate estimator under five prespecified threat families: covariate missingness, exposure misclassification, outcome misclassification, near-positivity, and unmeasured confounding.

In Monte Carlo experiments, adjusted estimators recovered the true risk difference under good overlap, and TMLE and cross-validated TMLE held bias small relative to the empirical standard deviation under marginal overlap. Under a deliberately misspecified outcome surface, cross-validated TMLE with a flexible library recovered the true risk difference, while the unadjusted crude estimator carried the wrong sign and the GLM-based adjusted estimators, though correctly signed, remained substantially biased. A supplementary variance comparison found that the matched-cohort TMLE paired-difference SE is anti-conservative under good overlap (95% CI coverage 0.89, Monte Carlo SE 0.03) because it ignores matching-draw variance, and a full-pipeline bootstrap that re-runs matching on each resample raised coverage to 0.95 (Abadie and Imbens 2008). select_variance_method() uses oracle coverage on plasmode-generated simulated data to identify, for each estimator-scenario combination, which variance method achieves nominal coverage. When unmeasured confounding was introduced, all estimators were biased in the same direction, and the prespecified pre-outcome decision correctly returned STOP: the workflow flags a prespecified unmeasured-confounding scenario under which the planned analysis would no longer meet the locked operating-characteristic thresholds. The data-quality stress test further showed that outcome misclassification and unmeasured confounding produced the largest degradation in estimator performance. The package also ships a worst-case selection rule (min_max_rmse) that ranks candidates by their maximum RMSE across all declared threats; a companion vignette illustrates a setting where this rule locks a different candidate from the baseline min_rmse rule.

We illustrate the workflow on the Rescue.Co Kenya Trauma Registry, five transport contrasts on 8,323 patients with known transport mode. The protocol’s primary comparison, Rescue.Co against all other transport, placed 41 percent of the sample outside the propensity band [0.05, 0.95] with a maximum inverse-probability weight above 250; the design stage graded it severe, refused the average treatment effect, and moved the analysis down the declared ladder to the trimmed, treated-population and overlap-weighted estimands, all before any outcome was joined. The two socioeconomic negative controls that fail on the full ambulance cohort turn null after the pre-registered transfer and prior-care exclusions, reproducing the parallel unblinded analysis to four decimals; the exclusions, not adjustment, removed the measurable confounding. cleanTMLE is the software layer of an outcome-blind staged workflow: it does not replace target-trial design, fit-for-purpose data review, validation studies, independent governance, or post-outcome sensitivity analyses. Its contribution is to make “is this comparison estimable, and with which estimand” a question the design team answers, with a reproducible record, before outcomes are unlocked.

Keywords: targeted maximum likelihood estimation, plasmode simulation, real-world evidence, positivity, estimand, outcome-blind analysis, R, statistical analysis plan, regulatory science.

1 Introduction

1.1 Two failure modes, one blind phase

Comparative analyses of real-world data fail in two ways that no amount of estimator sophistication repairs after the fact. The first is analyst degrees of freedom: when the person choosing the model can see how each choice moves the answer, the final estimate carries those peeks, however honest the person (Muntner et al. 2024). The second is quieter and worse. Some comparisons are not estimable at all, and the estimator does not say so. The average treatment effect asks what would have happened had everyone received treatment versus no one, and answering it requires that every kind of patient had a real chance of landing in either arm (Petersen et al. 2012). When a whole stratum essentially never receives one of the treatments, the estimator does not refuse; it extrapolates. In the trauma registry that motivates our case study (Section 12), a time-to-arrival analysis under exactly this condition produced an effect of +14,637 minutes inside a narrow confidence interval, against a crude difference of about seven hours in the opposite direction. Nothing in the estimator’s own output flags the failure. Weight truncation controls the variance without touching the extrapolation, so the interval stays narrow around a meaningless number.

The staged, outcome-blind (“clean-room”) design of Muntner et al. (2024) addresses the first failure: a design team defines the cohort, fits the propensity model, and completes the design diagnostics without seeing the outcome, and only then does an outcome team estimate. It does nothing about the second. A perfectly blinded team can still promise an estimand the data cannot deliver, and blinding, if anything, raises the stakes, because the promise is locked before the data can contradict it. The premise of this paper is that the blind phase is the right place to answer the estimability question: whether the declared comparison is estimable in these data, and if not, which neighbouring estimand is. The effect among the treated and the overlap-weighted effect reweight the same fitted propensity score with bounded weights (Li, Morgan, and Zaslavsky 2018; Mao, Li, and Greene 2019), so both can remain estimable where the average treatment effect is not, and a trimmed analysis changes the population, which the design team should profile and disclose (Crump et al. 2009). Deciding among these before outcome access, by a rule declared in advance, turns what is usually a silent post-hoc substitution into a documented design decision. Section 6 develops this into a graded support assessment, a per-estimand feasibility map, and a pre-registered estimand ladder.

1.2 Prespecification and fit-for-purpose data in RWE

Outcome blinding and prespecification are governance tools, not substitutes for causal design. In a real-world evidence (RWE) study the analyst still has to define the target trial (M. A. Hernán and Robins 2016; Miguel A. Hernán and Robins 2016), specify a statistical estimand consistent with the ICH E9(R1) framework (International Council for Harmonisation 2019), justify identification from the available data, and defend the relevance and reliability of the data source for the regulatory or scientific question.

Regulatory bodies have converged on this list. The FDA RWE framework and its source-specific guidances cover real-world data and evidence (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018, 2024a), EHR and claims data (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b), registries (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2021), and non-interventional studies (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024c). The EMA materials add registry-based studies (European Medicines Agency 2021), a regulator-led RWE guide (European Medicines Agency 2024), and an RWD data-quality framework (European Medicines Agency 2026). ICH M14 (March 2026) sets harmonised principles for non-interventional studies that use real-world data for safety assessment of medicines (International Council for Harmonisation 2026).

Within this broader workflow, two arguments are typically developed in parallel but reported separately. The estimator-selection argument is checked with outcome-blind plasmode simulation (Franklin et al. 2014; Schuler and Rose 2017; Dang et al. 2023; Gruber, Lee, et al. 2024; Schreck et al. 2024). The fit-for-purpose argument is documented qualitatively through templates such as SPIFD2, the Structured Process to Identify Fit-for-purpose study Design and Data (Gatto, Reynolds, and Campbell 2022; Gatto et al. 2023), or HARPER (Wang, Sreedhara, and Schneeweiss 2023), and through reporting tools such as TARGET, the Target Trial reporting tool for observational studies (Cashin et al. 2024), and STaRT-RWE, the Structured Template for Planning and Reporting on the Implementation of real-world evidence studies (Wang et al. 2021).

These two arguments are connected: a candidate estimator that performs well on a simulation derived from real covariate and treatment distributions may still fail under realistic measurement error, missingness, or unmeasured confounding. The plasmode loop is under the analyst’s control, so it can be extended to ask not only “which candidate has the lowest RMSE under the locked data-generating process?” but also “which candidate maintains acceptable bias, RMSE, and coverage across the plausible range of each threat documented in the fit-for-purpose review?” We refer to this extension as a data-quality (DQ) stress test. It is a pre-outcome robustness screen rather than a substitute for variable validation or for post-unblinding sensitivity analysis. The workflow does not guarantee that estimator rankings under simulated outcomes will generalise to the realised outcome process; the conclusions are only as credible as the simulated-outcome model and the externally justified severity ranges entered into the DQ stress test.

We use “data-quality stress testing” in a restricted sense: the procedure does not assess data provenance, phenotype validity, linkage accuracy, representativeness, or regulatory acceptability, which remain study-level evaluations. Once investigators have specified plausible threats and severity ranges from external validation studies, data profiling, or expert elicitation, the package evaluates how candidate estimators behave under those prespecified perturbations before the observed treatment-outcome association is examined. The central contribution is a quantitative bridge between fit-for-purpose review and estimator selection. In a conventional workflow, data-fitness concerns are documented qualitatively, while estimator choice is justified separately through modeling preferences or diagnostics. cleanTMLE uses the same outcome-blind plasmode loop used for candidate selection to evaluate whether prespecified TMLE candidates remain acceptable under data-quality threats derived from the fit-for-purpose review.

In this manuscript, outcome-blind means that decisions about cohort construction, candidate estimators, simulation scenarios, decision thresholds, and primary-estimator selection are made without inspecting the observed treatment-outcome association. Analysts may use baseline covariates, treatment assignment, missingness indicators, and simulated outcomes generated for plasmode simulations; the marginal mean of the observed outcome on covariates is also used internally to fit the plasmode generator. The observed treatment-outcome relationship is not used for estimator selection or design revision before the pre-outcome decision point.

A standard staged analysis often separates three activities: target-trial / protocol design, qualitative fit-for-purpose data review, and estimator selection. Standard plasmode simulation can compare estimators before outcome access, but it usually evaluates performance under one locked simulated outcome mechanism. cleanTMLE extends that loop by stress-testing the selected estimator across prespecified data-quality threats derived from the fit-for-purpose review. This builds a quantitative bridge between the qualitative data-fitness argument and the estimator-selection argument.

1.3 What the package adds, and what it does not

cleanTMLE is an R (R Core Team 2024) package that operationalises the design and estimator-selection steps of a staged analysis within the causal roadmap (Dang et al. 2023; Petersen and Laan 2014; Gruber, Lee, et al. 2024). It contributes three methodological components. The first is the estimability layer introduced above: a graded assessment of overlap on the fitted propensity score, a per-estimand feasibility reading of the same fit, an outcome-blind simulation that maps where each estimand’s estimator holds its operating characteristics, and a pre-registered estimand ladder that governs switching (Section 6). The second is an outcome-blind plasmode candidate selector, and the third is the data-quality stress test, which extends that selector to score each candidate against prespecified data-quality threats (Section 7). All three build on targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) (Laan and Rubin 2006; Laan and Rose 2011; Schuler and Rose 2017; Zheng and Laan 2011; Chernozhukov et al. 2018), the natural setting because every analytic decision (the SuperLearner library (Laan, Polley, and Hubbard 2007; Phillips et al. 2023), the truncation rule, the targeting procedure, and the prespecified set of candidate estimators) can be listed in advance, while the estimator remains data-adaptive and still admits valid Wald-type confidence intervals under standard regularity conditions. This modular structure makes it possible to compare prespecified candidates under simulated outcomes without revising the analytic plan after inspecting observed treatment-outcome associations.

Around these statistical components the package adds a transparency layer, for analysts who want their prespecification to be a reproducible record rather than a separate paper document: an analysis-lock object that fingerprints the specification and masks the outcome, and a design log that timestamps the ladder declaration, the support verdicts, and any estimand switch or override. The pre-outcome decision applies the three review-team recommendations of Muntner et al. (2024), namely proceeding to the comparative analysis, proceeding with a documented qualification or additional analysis, or stopping before it. Earlier versions of the package enforced this sequence by withholding the primary-analysis functions until every checkpoint had been recorded. The current version deletes that layer. The lock’s data frame never holds the primary outcome, which lives in a separate store that only the estimation stage joins back, and the one enforcement option that remains, enforce = TRUE, makes estimation refuse to run until a named approver restores the store, an approval the design log records (Section 5). This software arrangement sits inside, rather than substitutes for, the personnel-based governance of a clean room such as role separation, credentialed data access, and an independent masked review team, which we return to in Section 13. The “clean room” label is the manufacturing analogy adopted by Muntner et al. (2024), in which access to a sterile area is blocked until protocols have been followed; the substantive content here is the staged restriction of outcome access. Section 2 situates the package inside the causal roadmap.

1.4 Current scope of cleanTMLE

The simulation and case study in this paper run on a binary point exposure and a binary outcome. Within that setting the package now estimates a family of related estimands rather than a single one: the marginal risk difference for the average treatment effect (ATE), the trimmed ATE on the region of common support (Crump et al. 2009), the effect among the treated (ATT), the overlap-weighted effect (ATO) (Li, Morgan, and Zaslavsky 2018; Mao, Li, and Greene 2019), and a matched-cohort ATT sensitivity analysis. One front door, estimate_effect(), takes the estimand, the estimator family (TMLE, inverse-probability weighting, matching, or the crude contrast), and the missing-outcome handling (complete-case or inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting, IPCW) as arguments; the complete-case path is unbiased under missingness completely at random, and the IPCW path under conditional independent censoring given measured covariates and treatment. The prespecified primary estimator is TMLE, with the alternatives reported as concordance checks. Multi-arm exposures are handled as prespecified pairwise contrasts, each under its own lock on a shared cohort (create_contrast_locks()), which is how the case study analyses its five transport comparisons. A companion grammar of specify_models(), identify_*(), and estimate_*() verbs covers cumulative risks for time-to-event outcomes with censoring and competing risks. Time-varying treatments and native missingness-handling models (multiple imputation, inverse-probability-of-missingness weighting for covariates) remain out of scope, although the data-quality stress test degrades covariates under MAR and MNAR to test the default median-imputation handling against them. Analysts who need longitudinal estimands can compose cleanTMLE’s prespecification functions with survtmle (Benkeser and Hejazi 2018) or lmtp (Williams and Dı́az 2021). This paper documents version 0.3.0 of the package, whose workflow surface is sixteen verbs that run in stage order against one lock object: create_analysis_lock(), declare_negative_controls(), and declare_estimand_ladder() seal the plan; fit_ps(), assess_support(), estimand_feasibility(), and simulate_support() answer the estimability question; define_candidates(), stress_test(), and select_candidate() choose the estimator under declared threats; negative_control_ladder() and check_process_indicators() look for residual confounding; design_report() and export_design_log() produce what the review team reads; and estimate_effect() and run_estimand_ladder() estimate. Earlier versions accreted governance helpers faster than they earned their place, and the 0.2.0 consolidation and the 0.3.0 revision removed them. The case-study estimates in Section 12 were produced under version 0.2.0.

1.5 What the paper contributes

We state the contribution narrowly. It is not a new estimator or a new theorem: the estimators are standard targeted learning, the overlap diagnostics descend from Petersen et al. (2012), and prespecifying TMLE in a statistical analysis plan is already set out by Gruber, Lee, et al. (2024) and Step 5 of the roadmap (Dang et al. 2023). The contribution is a single, prespecified, outcome-blind procedure with three parts, together with a reproducible software implementation. First, the procedure makes estimand feasibility a design-stage output: the same fitted propensity score is read per estimand, an outcome-blind simulation maps where each estimand’s estimator holds a bias tolerance at near-nominal coverage, and a pre-registered ladder converts any switch into a logged design decision (Section 6). In building that simulation we adopt the generate-treatment plasmode design, because the common sample-treatment alternative, which keeps each subject’s observed treatment, induces a positivity violation by construction and misgrades exactly the designs the map is meant to grade (Shaw et al. 2025). Second, the procedure ties the qualitative fit-for-purpose threats documented in a SPIFD2-style review (Gatto et al. 2023) to quantitative estimator selection on one decision scale: we extend the outcome-blind plasmode loop (Dang et al. 2023; Gruber, Lee, et al. 2024; Schreck et al. 2024) from candidate-estimator selection to estimator robustness screening under prespecified threat ranges, so each candidate produces a degradation gradient on the same bias, RMSE, and coverage scale as the baseline plasmode and the prespecified decision rule applies uniformly across baseline and stressed scenarios. Third, we characterise the screen’s operating characteristics as a decision rule (Section 11): how often it returns the same proceed-or-stop verdict an oracle with knowledge of the realised estimator’s bias would return, and how that calibration degrades when the simulated-outcome model is misspecified.

The boundary with the FIORD framework is as follows. FIORD, the Forum on the Integration of Observational and Randomized Data (Nance et al. 2026; Kent 2026), supplies the outcome-blind candidate-evaluation loop and the two-stage selector that first screens candidates on oracle coverage and then selects a variance method. This paper contributes the software implementation of that loop, the data-quality stress-test extension that scores each candidate under prespecified threats on the same decision scale, and the lock, design-log, and pre-outcome-decision record. We hold to this division of labour throughout, and we do not claim the outcome-blind selection framework as original to this work.

We position the screen as a quantitative supplement to fit-for-purpose review (Section 8) and not a substitute for variable-validation studies, source-data assessment, or post-outcome quantitative bias analysis, and we are explicit (Section 8.5) about what passing it does and does not establish. The R implementation records the supporting prespecification (the SHA-256-fingerprinted analysis lock, the design log, and the pre-outcome decision) so that the screen and the locked primary analysis share a single reproducible record.

For an applied real-world evidence team the operational payoff is concrete. Prespecifying the estimand, the candidate estimators, the learner libraries, and the decision thresholds inside a fingerprinted lock, and recording every pre-outcome diagnostic in an exportable design log, gives a reviewer a record that can be reconstructed without relying on the analyst’s recollection of which choice was made when. This addresses a recurring concern in real-world evidence submissions, that analytic choices may have been shaped by the observed treatment-outcome association (Muntner et al. 2024). The same record reduces post-hoc disputes over truncation, learner library, and cohort decisions, because each is timestamped before the outcome is read. The cost is the discipline of fixing these choices in advance and the compute time of the plasmode and data-quality runs, both of which fit inside a conventional statistical-analysis-plan timeline.

The practical consequence is visible when the same fitted estimators are read under a conventional pipeline and under the staged workflow (Table 6). Under good overlap the two agree. Under marginal overlap the workflow flags the IPTW variance calibration before unblinding, where the conventional pipeline relies on a reviewer to notice it. Under unmeasured confounding of a prespecified strength the staged decision rule returns STOP and the locked primary analysis does not run, whereas the conventional pipeline reports an estimate biased toward the null (mean bias about 0.037 toward zero, roughly twice the 0.02 threshold, so the realised risk difference of about -0.005 attenuates the true -0.042), with 95% CI coverage of the true effect near 0.42 and only about 6% of replicate intervals excluding zero. A conventional analysis would therefore typically report no significant effect and publish a null that masks a real one. Under this prespecified unmeasured-confounding scenario the realised measured-covariate analysis is materially biased and under-covering, so both a realised-bias oracle and the outcome-blind screen flag it (detection and fragility agree), and a conventional pipeline would publish a misleading null. The fits are identical under both pipelines; the difference is the prespecified decision applied before the outcome is read.

1.6 Why targeted learning for an outcome-blind workflow

An outcome-blind workflow fixes the estimator before the treatment-outcome association is read, so the estimator must have a target that is declared in advance and that does not depend on how the nuisance models are fit. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation has this structure. The target parameter, here the marginal risk difference, is specified before estimation, and the propensity-score and outcome models are nuisance fits that can be learned by flexible, data-adaptive methods without changing the target. The targeting step then removes the plug-in bias of the initial outcome fit using the propensity score, so the bias of the final estimator does not depend on the quality of any single nuisance model in the way a plug-in or single-model estimator does. This double-robustness property, that a consistent estimate follows if either the propensity or the outcome model is correctly specified, is shared with augmented inverse-probability weighting. The candidate estimators are enumerable, which is what makes outcome-blind selection among them feasible: each candidate is a fixed choice of nuisance libraries, truncation, and cross-fitting, and the candidates can be ranked on simulated data before the outcome is unblinded. A logistic outcome regression or an inverse-probability weight does not separate the target from the model in this way, which is why the workflow is built on targeted learning.

The next section (Section 2) places these contributions inside the causal roadmap, and subsequent sections follow that roadmap order.

2 The causal roadmap and the role of cleanTMLE

cleanTMLE is designed to encourage the analyst to follow the causal roadmap of Petersen and Laan (2014) and Dang et al. (2023) when defining and executing the analysis. The roadmap sets out an explicit, prespecified sequence of seven steps: (1) state the causal question, causal model, and causal estimand; (2) characterise the observed data and their fitness for the target trial; (3) assess identifiability; (4) define the statistical estimand; (5) choose a statistical model and estimator with prespecified operating characteristics, using outcome-blind simulation and targeted learning; (6) specify a procedure for sensitivity analysis to violations of the identification assumptions; and (7) compare alternative study designs, again using outcome-blind simulation (Dang et al. 2023). The package applies this roadmap to a staged analysis in the sense of Muntner et al. (2024). It operationalises Step 5 through outcome-blind plasmode estimator selection and TMLE estimators, contributes the data-quality stress test as an extension of Steps 5 and 7, and records the Step 6 sensitivity analyses. The support assessment and estimand ladder of Section 6 operationalise the positivity portion of Step 3 and the estimand revision that Step 4 requires when identification fails in the practical sense (Petersen et al. 2012). The remainder of Steps 1 to 4 is external study-level work, supported by target-trial templates (M. A. Hernán and Robins 2016; Cashin et al. 2024), fit-for-purpose checklists (Gatto et al. 2023; Wang, Sreedhara, and Schneeweiss 2023), and source-specific data-relevance and reliability assessments (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a, 2024b, 2021; European Medicines Agency 2024, 2026).

To keep the estimand, estimator, simulation, and governance decision distinct, the manuscript uses a fixed vocabulary for the conceptual layers of the workflow, defined in Table 14 (Appendix). Figure 7 (Appendix) places the package inside the roadmap, shading the steps it can operationalise, and Figure 8 situates the software arrangement within the broader governance stack of external validation, independent oversight, and data standards. A full mapping of each roadmap component to the relevant FDA, EMA, and ICH expectation, to what cleanTMLE operationalises in software, and to what still requires external study-level justification is given in Table 15, and Table 16 lists the additional event-process and diagnostic helpers. We return to the regulatory correspondence in Section 13 instead of developing it in the methods, because the software operationalises only part of each expectation.

The remaining methods sections follow the roadmap order. Section 4 states the target-trial estimand and identification assumptions used in the simulation. Section 5 describes the staged workflow and the lock and design-log records. Section 6 develops the support assessment, the per-estimand feasibility map, and the estimand ladder, the design-stage answer to the estimability question. Section 7 introduces the DQ stress test, including a threat-to-assumption matrix that is explicit about what each scenario probes and what it does not probe, and discusses calibration of severity ranges from external evidence. Section 8 reframes the DQ stress test as a quantitative supplement to fit-for-purpose review rather than a replacement for it. Section 9–Section 12 report the implementation, the simulation, and the case study; Section 13 discusses limitations and the role of post-outcome sensitivity analyses.

3 cleanTMLE at a glance: a worked walkthrough

Before developing the estimand, the framework, and the stress test formally, we show the package used end-to-end, so that later sections can be read against a concrete sequence of calls and outputs. The walkthrough follows the Rescue.Co case study of Section 12, with the code kept schematic and representative output shown inline; the full results are deferred to that section. The workflow is a small number of verbs. Everything before run_estimand_ladder() runs with no outcome access, and the outcome columns are physically absent from the design stage in the case study (they live in a separate store until estimation).

Show R code 
library(cleanTMLE)

# Lock the specification and declare intent before outcome access: the
# primary estimand, the fallbacks, and the trigger that moves the
# analysis down the ladder.
lock <- create_analysis_lock(
  data = rescueco, treatment = "rescueco", outcome = "death_by_6mo",
  covariates = design_columns,
  negative_controls = c("nc_household_urban", "nc_chronic_hypertension"),
  mask = TRUE, seed = 2026)
lock <- declare_estimand_ladder(
  lock, primary = "ATE", fallbacks = c("trimmed_ATE", "ATT", "ATO"),
  trigger = "SEVERE", bias_to_null_floor = 0.0035)

# The design stage: fit the propensity, grade the support, read the same
# fit per estimand, and map feasibility with an outcome-blind simulation.
ps  <- fit_ps(lock)
sup <- assess_support(ps)
#> 40.6% outside [0.05, 0.95]; max weight 257; verdict SEVERE
fea <- estimand_feasibility(ps, profile_vars = interpretable_vars)
#> ATE infeasible; ATT max control weight 5.0; ATO weights bounded by 1
sim <- simulate_support(lock, ps, reps = 200)
design_report(lock, sup, fea, sim)
#> The declared primary (ATE) is NOT supported (overlap verdict SEVERE).
#> The ladder moves to: trimmed_ATE, then ATT, then ATO. The switch is a
#> logged design decision.

# Estimation: outcomes are joined only now. The declared primary runs when
# feasible plus every feasible fallback; every row carries its estimand,
# the support verdict, and the implausibility flags, and every switch or
# override is logged.
fit <- run_estimand_ladder(lock, ps)

Table 1 summarises the functions the workflow exercises, what each one does, and the representative output it returns. Candidate selection and the data-quality stress test (Section 7) slot in between the support assessment and estimation through the same lock. A lock created with enforce = TRUE refuses estimation until unmask_outcome() restores the outcome store with a named approved_by, and that approval is a design-log entry; whatever the setting, the lock’s data frame never holds the primary outcome.

4 Estimand, Causal Model, and Identifiability

4.1 Estimand specification

We follow International Council for Harmonisation (2019) and Dang et al. (2023) by writing the estimand along five attributes. For the running example the population is adults eligible at the index visit. The treatment is a binary point exposure \(A \in \{0, 1\}\) at index. The endpoint is a binary indicator of the primary event by 24 months, denoted \(Y\). The summary measure is the marginal counterfactual risk difference \(\Psi = E\{Y(1)\} - E\{Y(0)\}\). Intercurrent events are handled under a treatment-policy strategy; censoring and treatment switching are not modelled in this illustration. The corresponding statistical estimand under the identification assumptions in Section 4.4 is \(\Psi = E_W\{E[Y \mid A=1, W] - E[Y \mid A=0, W]\}\), the marginal g-formula contrast (J. Robins 1986; Miguel A. Hernán and Robins 2020).

In the workflow this specification is recorded on the lock at Stage 1a, as the estimand argument of create_analysis_lock(), and is preserved on the lock object that downstream stages consume. The estimand fields are metadata outside the integrity fingerprint, which digests the design data and the analytic specification; the exported design log carries the ladder declaration and every later switch, so the estimand the analysis ends up reporting can be traced from the declaration to the estimate.

4.2 Causal model

The data-generating process has five baseline covariates \(W = (\text{age}, \text{sex}, \text{biomarker}, \text{comorbidity}, \text{CKD})\), a binary treatment \(A\) that depends on \(W\), and a binary outcome \(Y\) at 24 months. In the unmeasured-confounding scenario a binary \(U \sim \text{Bern}(p_U)\) also affects both \(A\) and \(Y\). The DAG is

   W ───► A ──► Y
   │          ▲
   └──────────┘
   (Scenario C only:)
   U ──► A
   U ──► Y

with no arrow from \(A\) to \(W\) (point exposure) and no arrow between \(W\) and \(U\).

4.3 Event-process classification

A recurring source of ambiguity in real-world evidence analyses is the treatment of post-baseline events such as treatment discontinuation, treatment switching, death, loss to follow-up, administrative end of follow-up, and missing outcome measurement. These events should not be assigned generically to censoring or exclusion rules. Instead, each event should be mapped to its role in the causal estimand, its corresponding ICH E9(R1) intercurrent-event strategy when applicable, and its operational role in estimation. For example, death may be an outcome, a competing event, a component of a composite endpoint, or an intercurrent event requiring a treatment-policy, hypothetical, composite, while-on-treatment, or principal-stratum strategy, depending on the clinical question. This classification should be prespecified and linked to sensitivity analyses, and recorded as a structured object that the design log can carry.

4.4 Identifiability assumptions

Under this DAG, \(\Psi\) is identified by the g-formula if three identification assumptions hold (Miguel A. Hernán and Robins 2020):

  • Conditional exchangeability, \(Y(a) \perp\!\!\!\perp A \mid W\). This holds in scenarios A and B by construction. It is violated by construction in scenario C, where \(U\) is not in the analyst’s adjustment set. Probed by: the unmeasured-confounding scenario in stress_test().
  • Positivity, \(0 < \Pr(A = 1 \mid W) < 1\) for every \(W\) in the support. Scenario A satisfies this comfortably. Scenario B pushes the propensity toward the boundary but does not violate it in the limit. Probed by: the near-positivity scenario, which amplifies the covariate-to-treatment association, and by the truncation level of each TMLE candidate; near-positivity strain shows up as inflated SE/SD in the baseline plasmode metrics. In finite samples the binding form of this assumption is practical positivity (Petersen et al. 2012), which Section 6 treats as a first-class design question with its own diagnostics, per-estimand feasibility reading, and estimand ladder.
  • Consistency / SUTVA, \(Y = Y(A)\). Probed by: the treatment- misclassification scenario, which simulates a violation of consistency caused by exposure-algorithm error.

Identification of \(\Psi\) requires only these three. It does not require that the nuisance models be correctly specified: that is the point of targeted learning, whose targeting step keeps the estimator consistent when the outcome model is misspecified but the propensity model is not, and vice versa. Two further conditions are needed for the estimate to be trustworthy rather than merely identified, and the DQ stress test probes them alongside the identification assumptions above. These are measurement and estimation conditions, not identification assumptions:

  • No measurement error in the outcome, \(\tilde{Y} = Y\), and no differential exposure or outcome misclassification. Probed by: the outcome-misclassification scenario, with optional per-arm differential misclassification.
  • Covariate missingness that median imputation can absorb. The stress test degrades \(W\) under MCAR, MAR, and MNAR masks . Probed by: the covariate-missingness scenario, which masks a fraction of values and imputes with the column median.

Estimation quality, the choice of SuperLearner library and truncation rule for \(g(W)\) and \(E[Y \mid A, W]\), is not an identification assumption either; it is exercised by the standard plasmode candidate-selection metrics, which compare candidates that vary the library and the truncation rule.

The simulation thus contains one analytic challenge (marginal overlap, B) and one identifiability violation (unmeasured confounding, C). We use C to demonstrate what the DQ stress test flags under a prespecified latent-U scenario, and to contrast the stress-test output with the post-hoc E-value (VanderWeele and Ding 2017) and with the negative-control-outcome check (Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen, and Cohen 2010).

5 The cleanTMLE Framework

5.1 Staged workflow

cleanTMLE adopts the staged design set out by Muntner et al. (2024) and aligns it with the causal-roadmap formulation of Dang et al. (2023) and the targeted-learning statistical-analysis-plan template of Gruber, Lee, et al. (2024). Stage names below are package-internal labels; the stage content matches the roadmap steps of Dang et al. (2023).

Stage Purpose Does the function read the outcome?
0 Feasibility assessment, utilisation study, draft protocol/SAP (Muntner et al. 2024; Kent 2026) No (no data access yet)
1a Lock covariates, learner library, candidate grid; declare the estimand ladder No
1b Cohort adequacy: \(N\) per arm, events, design precision Events only
2a Propensity fit, support assessment, per-estimand feasibility, balance (Section 6) No
2b Outcome-blind support map and plasmode candidate selection No (simulated outcome)
2c Plasmode DQ stress test No (simulated outcome)
3 Negative-control ladder, process-indicator (collider) check NC outcomes only
Pre-outcome decision Design report: proceed, proceed with qualification, or stop No
4 Estimation of the declared primary and feasible fallbacks Yes

Stages 1 to 3 do not access the real outcome. The plasmode at Stage 2b resamples the real covariates, redraws treatment from the fitted propensity, and generates simulated outcomes from a covariate-only baseline surface (fitted on the real outcome given covariates in the hybrid generator mode, or supplied from pilot data in the external-pilot mode) with the treatment effect injected, which is why the same loop hosts both the support map of Section 6 and the DQ stress test of Section 7.

Within a staging-and-clean-room framework, the DQ stress test is a quantitative checkpoint. Instead of discussing data-fitness concerns only qualitatively, the workflow evaluates whether candidate estimators continue to satisfy prespecified operating-characteristic thresholds under threat scenarios derived from the fit-for-purpose review.

Clean-room guidance addresses a limitation of preregistration: during RWE execution, investigators often encounter data incompleteness, coding limitations, sparse events, covariate imbalance, model-convergence problems, and censoring or missingness issues that require decisions after data access but before comparative effect estimation (McGrath et al. 2021; Muntner et al. 2024). cleanTMLE operationalises the software portion of this process by recording pre-outcome diagnostics, decisions, deviations, and the named unmasking approval in the design log before the observed primary treatment-outcome association is estimated.

5.2 How the workflow records and protects analytic decisions

The analysis lock is the central object on which all later diagnostics depend. It is created at the start of the workflow and records the prespecified analytic specification: the analytic dataset, the treatment, outcome, and covariate column names, the registered negative controls, the nuisance-learning library, and the random seed, together with any decision rules declared at creation (the data-quality thresholds dq_thresholds and the negative-control criteria nc_criteria). A SHA-256 fingerprint of those fields and of the content of every design column is recorded so that the same lock can be reconciled later by an external reviewer; the primary outcome is excluded from the digest, so masking and unmasking leave the hash unchanged while any edit to the design data changes it. The estimand ladder is attached to the lock by declare_estimand_ladder() and is captured by the design log, not by the fingerprint, so any later change to the ladder appears as a separate, timestamped entry. The lock splits its input at creation: the data frame the design verbs read holds design data only, and the primary outcome lives in a separate store that the estimation stage joins back after its guard. mask_outcome() removes the store, so a masked lock is physically outcome-free wherever it travels, and the package’s test suite asserts that the design verbs return identical output on a masked lock and under a permuted outcome; for the plasmode stage that identity holds in the external-pilot generator mode, since the hybrid mode fits its covariate-only baseline surface on the real outcome (see the tradeoffs below).

The design log tracks analytic decisions through the workflow. It accumulates entries automatically from the diagnostics, recording what was evaluated, when, and against which prespecified criteria, and it captures analyst choices and any deviations from the protocol, with a brief rationale for each. The log can be exported as a tidy data frame and archived alongside the lock, so deviations from the recorded workflow can be detected during review. The exported record follows the structure of the Romiplostim worked example (McGrath et al. 2021), which Muntner et al. (2024) take as the reference template for a staged outcome-blind decision record, and export_design_log(format = "muntner") writes it in that template’s columns (date, stage, issue, decision, rationale, decided by). Earlier versions of the package additionally withheld the estimation functions until an authorisation token matching the lock and an audit record had been minted. Version 0.3.0 deletes that layer. The token ceremony, in our experience and in the case study, documented compliance without changing any analytic decision, and a determined analyst could always have bypassed it outside the package. What remains is one institutional switch: a lock created with enforce = TRUE refuses estimation until unmask_outcome() restores the outcome store with a named approved_by, and the design log records who approved and when.

In addition to a single outcome-masking step, Muntner et al. (2024) and Kent (2026) recommend tiered, role-based access in which analytic advisors see summary outputs by stage and checkpoint reviewers see summary outputs only by checkpoint. The design report and the exported design log support that arrangement at the workflow level, providing reviewer-facing summaries that do not require raw-data access.

5.3 Personnel-based and simulation-based outcome blinding

Outcome blinding can be enforced in two complementary ways. The first is personnel-based (Muntner et al. 2024). A blinded analyst writes the analysis plan, defines the cohort, performs the design diagnostics, and reaches the pre-outcome decision point; only then does a separate analyst, or another role on the same team, link the outcome and run the comparative analysis. Separation is maintained by an institutional partition of duties and a documented audit by a data manager who controls access to the outcome variable. Reviewers and regulators evaluate two documents at the end: a timestamped analysis plan and a final estimate produced under that plan.

Outcome-blind simulation addresses the same concern through a different mechanism. Candidate estimators, truncation rules, and data-quality scenarios may be evaluated using simulated outcomes generated without using the observed treatment-outcome association. This allows investigators to compare estimators and revise prespecified simulation settings before unblinding while preserving separation from the observed comparative effect. The software-mediated workflow partially substitutes for personnel-based outcome separation by restricting outcome analysis until prespecified review steps have been completed. It complements that arrangement: the design log sits alongside the timestamped paper plan and the data manager’s role, so reviewers see transparent documentation of every analytic decision on top of the institutional documentation that already exists.

The two arrangements address the same underlying concern, that analytic decisions made after seeing the treatment-outcome association are not credible, but they differ in their residual risks. Personnel-based blinding requires an institutional commitment to the partition of duties and tolerates ad-hoc deviation by the blinded analyst, since the only ground truth is the timestamped plan. Simulation-based blinding reduces the personnel constraint but introduces a different residual risk: the investigator must defend the assumption that the simulated-outcome mechanism is faithful enough to the real data-generating process that estimator selection on simulations generalises to the realised data. A defensible RWE pipeline can therefore use both, running the simulation-based workflow inside an institutional partition of duties so that outcome separation and quantitative robustness screening apply together.

5.3.1 Methodological tradeoffs

Compared with personnel-mediated outcome blinding, the simulation-mediated approach has the following tradeoffs.

In favour: a single statistician can produce a documented prespecification without a separate unblinded role, with the caveat that submission-grade studies should retain a personnel partition; the prespecified set of candidate estimators, the truncation thresholds, and the decision thresholds can be revised after viewing simulation results because those results use simulated outcomes, so the analytic plan need not be re-frozen each time a tuning choice is reconsidered; the design records support transparent reconstruction of every prespecified decision by an external reviewer; and the same simulation loop that selects the candidate can be used to evaluate its robustness to prespecified data-quality threats, an evaluation that has no direct counterpart in personnel-based blinding, where data fitness is documented qualitatively.

Against: the plasmode generator uses the realised outcome \(Y\) to fit a covariate-only mean model, so the analyst learns the marginal distribution of \(Y\) given \(W\), although not the joint \((A, Y) \mid W\) relationship. The Dang causal-roadmap reading of outcome-blind permits this; a stricter reading of outcome blinding would require \(E[Y \mid W]\) to come from external pilot data (Dang et al. 2023, 7), and the package supports both modes, recording which mode was used. The simulated outcome is generated from a parametric model with a fixed risk difference, so effect modification is not represented; a richer data-generating process is possible but is not exercised here. Finally, when the analyst also writes the plasmode and stress-test specifications, there is no independent check that the simulated-outcome mechanism is faithful, whereas the personnel-based arrangement provides an additional layer of cross-validation through the data manager.

We document these trade-offs explicitly in the package’s documentation so that the analyst can choose the level of formality the study requires. For exploratory or lower-stakes RWE studies, the software-only workflow may be adequate to document and audit outcome-blind estimator selection. For high-stakes regulatory or confirmatory studies, cleanTMLE should be embedded within personnel-based outcome-blinding and access-control arrangements.

5.4 Reviewer-facing pre-outcome study dossier

The pre-outcome study dossier is the structured bundle the review team reads before outcomes are unlocked. design_report() assembles it and closes with a one-line recommendation in the vocabulary of Muntner et al. (2024) (proceed, proceed with qualification, or stop) and a TARGET-style emulation table (Cashin et al. 2024) when the protocol components are supplied. Its components are:

Component cleanTMLE output Outcome access
Protocol and target-trial timing Lock record + design_report(protocol = ...) emulation table No Y
Cohort flow / attrition attrition_table() No Y
Covariate and missingness summary make_table1(), sanitize_covariates() report No Y
PS overlap, support verdict, balance fit_ps(), assess_support(), love_plot() No Y
Estimand feasibility and declared ladder estimand_feasibility(), declare_estimand_ladder() No Y
Weight diagnostics clean_weight_diagnostics() No Y
Event-count and precision adequacy estimate_design_precision() Marginal Y only
Outcome-blind support map simulate_support() Simulated Y only
Plasmode candidate selection define_candidates(), stress_test(), select_candidate() Simulated Y only
DQ stress-test results stress_test() Simulated Y only
Negative controls across cohort restrictions negative_control_ladder() Negative-control Y only
Care-process collider check check_process_indicators() No Y
Design log export export_design_log() No Y

The dossier is the document the reviewer reads. Comparative treatment-outcome estimates are not part of the dossier and are produced only after the review.

6 Deciding the estimand before outcomes

6.1 Practical positivity and why blinding does not detect it

The identification argument of Section 4.4 includes positivity: every covariate pattern in the target population must have a positive probability of receiving each treatment. In finite samples the binding version of this assumption is practical, not theoretical (Petersen et al. 2012). When the fitted propensity score \(g(W)\) approaches 0 or 1 in some region, the inverse-probability weights \(1/g\) and \(1/(1-g)\) that the ATE implicitly assigns become enormous, and the estimator answers the counterfactual question in that region by extrapolating the outcome model into territory where only one arm was ever observed. Truncating the weights (or bounding \(g\)) caps the variance but does not restore information; it trades an exploding interval for a stable interval around a partly extrapolated number. This is the second failure mode of the Introduction, and it is the one outcome blinding cannot touch. Blinding governs who sees what; the support of the design is a property of the covariate and treatment data that the blinded team already holds. The design stage is therefore the natural place to assess it, and the assessment costs no blinding at all, because none of the quantities involved read the outcome.

cleanTMLE makes this assessment a first-class stage with three outputs: a graded support verdict, a per-estimand feasibility table on the same fitted propensity, and an outcome-blind simulation that maps how much the residual extrapolation would matter. A pre-registered estimand ladder then converts the map into a decision.

6.2 Graded support assessment

assess_support() reads a fitted propensity object from fit_ps() and grades the overlap between arms. The headline statistics are the share of the sample with untruncated \(g(W)\) outside a prespecified band (default \([0.05, 0.95]\)), the largest implied ATE weight, the effective sample size per arm, and the c-statistic of the propensity fit, whose discrimination here is bad news rather than good: a propensity model that separates the arms almost perfectly is describing a design with almost no equipoise. The verdict is PASS, FLAG (more than 1% outside the band, or a maximum weight above 30), SEVERE (more than 25% outside, or a maximum weight above 150), or FAIL (more than 60% outside, or a maximum weight above 1000), and the verdict’s caveat sentence travels with every downstream estimate instead of living in a diagnostic file nobody reopens. The default thresholds are deliberately coarse; they are stated in the lock and can be overridden there, so a study that overrides them does so on the record.

Global statistics can pass while one stratum is starved, so two local checks run beside them. A stratum scan over the discrete covariates looks for cells in which treatment is nearly deterministic, and a shallow regression tree fitted to an indicator of extreme propensity searches for interaction-defined regions the scan would miss and reports each violation region with its size and treatment share. Either check can escalate the verdict. The associated plot is a mirrored histogram, treated propensities above the axis and controls below with the band shaded, chosen because non-overlap is visible in it at a glance and reviewers do not need training to read it.

6.3 Reading the same fit per estimand

Different estimands reweight the same fitted propensity differently, which is what gives the design team room to move when the ATE is not supported. estimand_feasibility() computes, from one ps_fit, the weight distribution each estimand implies, its maximum, the effective sample size by arm, the share of the sample effectively removed, and a per-estimand verdict on the same PASS to FAIL scale.

The trimmed ATE restricts to the region of common support, by a fixed band or by the variance-minimising rule of Crump et al. (2009), and then refits within it. Trimming changes the population, so the feasibility table is paired with a profile of who is removed: estimand_feasibility(profile_vars = ...) compares the trimmed-away patients with the retained ones on interpretable variables, and the design report states the retained population in words. The ATT reweights only controls, by \(g/(1-g)\) (the weighting representation in Li, Morgan, and Zaslavsky 2018), and the ATO weights every patient by the probability of the treatment they did not receive, so it targets the population in clinical equipoise with weights bounded by 1 (Li, Morgan, and Zaslavsky 2018; Mao, Li, and Greene 2019). A matched-cohort ATT rides along as a sensitivity analysis. Estimation for each rung uses the estimator suited to it: TMLE for the ATE and trimmed ATE (with IPCW available for missing outcomes), a complete-case TMLE for the ATT (the ATT efficient influence function does not compose with the IPCW censoring weights in our implementation, and the package says so rather than silently proceeding), and the augmented overlap-weighted estimator of Mao, Li, and Greene (2019) for the ATO.

6.4 The outcome-blind support map

The feasibility table says which estimands imply bounded weights. It cannot say how much the residual extrapolation matters, because that depends on how the outcome behaves in the region only one arm inhabits, and the design team is blind to the outcome. The package’s answer is the same plasmode device it uses for candidate selection. simulate_support() resamples the locked covariates, draws treatment from the fitted propensity, and generates simulated outcomes from a prespecified family of surfaces indexed by two knobs: how strongly the outcome depends on the direction that drives the non-overlap, and how much the treatment effect varies along that direction. Because the truth is known on every replicate, and known separately for the ATE, trimmed ATE, ATT, ATO, and matched estimands, the output is a support map: for each estimand, the region of the surface family in which its estimator stays within a prespecified bias tolerance at near-nominal coverage. An estimand whose estimator fails inside the plausible region of that family is declared infeasible, and the team learns this without touching a real outcome. The map is read jointly with the prespecified plausible region; a whole-grid pass rule is conservative by construction, and the design report states which rule was declared.

6.4.1 Generate-treatment versus sample-treatment

One design choice in this simulation needs stating, because the literature has recently shown it is easy to get wrong. Plasmode studies commonly resample covariate-treatment pairs, so each subject keeps their observed treatment. Shaw et al. (2025) show that this sample-treatment design builds a positivity violation into the simulation itself: covariate regions that are all-treated in the data stay all-treated in every replicate regardless of the generating propensity, so the simulation reproduces the observed violation rather than letting the declared design govern it. For most plasmode uses this is a nuisance. For a support map it is disqualifying, since the object under study is the violation. simulate_support() and the plasmode selector therefore default to the generate-treatment design: covariates are resampled, treatment is redrawn from the fitted propensity, and simulated outcomes follow. The sample-treatment design remains available as an explicit option for backward comparison, and the case study reports the two side by side on its primary contrast.

6.5 The estimand ladder

The remaining question is who decides what happens when the primary estimand fails, and when. Switching estimands after seeing results is a garden of forking paths; refusing ever to switch wastes designs that can support a neighbouring question. The package’s resolution is a pre-registered ladder. declare_estimand_ladder() records, on the lock and before any outcome access, the primary estimand, the ordered fallbacks, the support verdict that triggers a move (default SEVERE), and optional sensitivity floors such as the minimum bias-to-null that would overturn a conclusion. run_estimand_ladder() then estimates the declared primary whenever it is feasible, plus every feasible fallback, and labels each row with its estimand, its support verdict, and the trigger status. An infeasible primary is refused unless the analyst supplies an override reason, which is logged. The switch is thereby a design decision with a timestamp, not a silent substitution, and the reader of the final table can see what was promised, what was delivered, and why they differ.

Every estimate the ladder returns also passes an implausibility guard: a set of cheap checks against bounds the data imposes (an estimate whose sign contradicts the crude difference by an order of magnitude, exceeds several multiples of the crude contrast, or implies an arm-specific risk outside the observed range is flagged, not suppressed). The guard exists because the motivating failure, the +14,637-minute effect of the Introduction, would have been caught by any one of these checks, and none of them requires anything beyond the estimate and the raw arm summaries.

6.6 Negative-control ladder and process indicators

Two further design checks run beside the support machinery, both registered on the lock. The negative-control ladder fits every registered negative-control outcome on every nested cohort restriction, so the team sees not only whether a control fails but which restriction makes it pass; a control that fails on the full cohort and turns null after a pre-registered exclusion localises the confounding to the excluded stratum rather than leaving a global verdict (Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen, and Cohen 2010; Shi, Miao, and Tchetgen Tchetgen 2020). The process-indicator check regresses each care-process variable on treatment given severity, a collider alarm for conditioning on post-treatment care processes. Both reports enter the design dossier of Section 5.

7 Data Quality as a Quantifiable Threat

The outcome-blind plasmode loop on which the DQ stress test is built follows the guidance of Nance et al. (2026), which formalises a five-step pre-outcome candidate-evaluation procedure: (1) declare the candidate estimators, learner libraries, truncation grids, and variance methods to be compared; (2) specify a data-generating process; (3) generate replicates and apply candidate estimators factorially; (4) select candidates in two stages, first the point estimator (against an oracle-coverage screen built from the Monte Carlo empirical SE), then the variance method; (5) implement on real data and report transparently. FIORD also formalises a spectrum of data-generating processes for the simulation, from fully investigator-specified parametric structural equations, through hybrid generators that use empirical covariates and fitted treatment / censoring mechanisms with an investigator-specified outcome regression, to parametric bootstraps from the fitted joint. cleanTMLE’s default plasmode sits in the hybrid middle of this spectrum: it uses the empirical \((W, A)\) structure with a covariate-only outcome model, never the joint \((A, Y) \mid W\) relationship. The DQ stress test extends FIORD by adding the prespecified perturbation step on top of the same hybrid generator.

7.1 Why plasmode DQ stress testing adds information beyond standard pre-outcome diagnostics

Four pre-outcome tools answer four different questions and are complementary rather than substitutable. (i) Propensity-score diagnostics (Austin 2009) assess empirical comparability, overlap, and weight stability, indicating whether the design is feasible under the observed covariate and treatment distributions; they do not estimate the operating characteristics of a candidate estimator. Balance is conventionally summarised with standardised mean differences (SMDs), but univariate SMDs compare only the marginal means of each covariate and can be satisfied while variances, higher moments, or covariate interactions remain imbalanced, so distributional and interaction diagnostics are needed alongside them after matching or weighting (Austin 2009; Zhang et al. 2019). (ii) Baseline plasmode simulation evaluates candidate-estimator operating characteristics (bias, RMSE, coverage) under a single locked simulated outcome model conditional on the empirical \((W, A)\) structure. (iii) Negative-control analyses probe residual bias for selected control outcomes against a different data-generating channel altogether; they do not directly evaluate how the primary estimator behaves under prespecified measurement error, missingness, or unmeasured-confounding scenarios. (iv) The DQ stress test asks whether the locked estimator-selection decision is stable under prespecified fit-for-purpose threats translated into quantitative perturbations of the baseline plasmode, before the primary treatment-outcome association is inspected. A STOP under a stress scenario should be read as evidence that the study requires redesign, external validation, additional sensitivity analysis, or narrower causal claims before outcome access.

The DQ stress test is a quantitative supplement to fit-for-purpose review, not a substitute for validation, governance, or post-outcome quantitative bias analysis. The workflow does not guarantee that estimator rankings under simulated outcomes will generalise to the realised outcome process. DQ stress testing should not be interpreted as a formal identification-region analysis or as a replacement for post-outcome quantitative bias analysis. It is a pre-outcome robustness screen for estimator behaviour under prespecified perturbations.

7.2 Mapping data-quality concerns to plasmode parameters

SPIFD2 (Gatto et al. 2023) does not list a fixed taxonomy of “data-quality dimensions”; it is a stepwise template that asks the analyst to record each design element of the hypothetical target trial and the data feature that operationalises it. The harmonised data-quality terminology of Kahn et al. (2016), by contrast, defines three dimensions (conformance, completeness, plausibility) that have become standard in OHDSI-style assessments. We map both SPIFD2 design-element categories and the Kahn et al. (2016) dimensions to plasmode parameters as follows.

The mapping is deliberately one-to-many: a single SPIFD2 design element (say, outcome ascertainment) can drive several plasmode parameters (per-arm sensitivity and specificity), and a single plasmode parameter (say, MCAR fraction) can speak to several SPIFD2 elements (covariate availability, missingness handling).

7.3 The degradation gradient

Rather than testing a single value of each threat, the function sweeps a vector of severities. The degradation gradient is the curve of bias, RMSE, coverage, or type I error against the severity of a prespecified data-quality threat. It is analogous to a dose-response curve for estimator fragility: it asks how severe the degradation must be before a candidate fails the locked decision criteria. A robust candidate has a shallow gradient and remains within thresholds across plausible severities. A fragile candidate shows a cliff, where a small increase in degradation moves bias or coverage beyond the threshold. The default candidate-selection rule (select_candidate(rule = "min_rmse")) chooses on RMSE in a single step. cleanTMLE also provides rule = "fiord_two_stage", which implements the point-estimator stage of the two-stage selector formalised in FIORD (Nance et al. 2026): candidates are first screened to those that achieve nominal oracle coverage (a CI built from the Monte Carlo empirical SE), and the lowest-variance survivor is locked in. FIORD’s second stage, selecting the variance method on the locked point estimator to achieve nominal coverage, is provided by select_variance_method(), with bootstrap_rd_variance() supplying a full-pipeline nonparametric bootstrap that re-runs matching on each resample as one candidate variance method alongside the influence-function SE; the method achieving nominal oracle coverage is selected empirically (Section 10). The rule can also require a maximum allowed degradation in the DQ stress test, which excludes fragile candidates before the outcome is accessed.

Propensity-score truncation does not only stabilise variance. It also restricts support to units with adequate overlap and therefore changes the effective target population, so it changes the estimand and not only the variance of the estimator (Lash et al. 2014). When the prespecified truncation level varies across candidates, the candidates are paired estimator-and-estimand objects, and the pre-outcome decision must consider whether the implied target population still answers the scientific question posed in the target trial. cleanTMLE records the truncation rule for each candidate as part of the analysis lock, so the estimand-versus-estimator distinction is auditable and any estimand drift induced by truncation is scored on the same RMSE and coverage metrics as everything else, and not chosen post-hoc on the realised data.

7.3.1 When STOP motivates estimand revision, not just estimator

swapping

A STOP or FLAG decision from the pre-outcome rule is not always a signal to change the estimator; sometimes it is a signal to change the estimand itself. The targeted-learning RWE roadmap (Dang et al. 2023; Petersen and Laan 2014) makes this explicit: if the simulation reveals that no prespecified candidate can recover the original target estimand under plausible threats, the honest moves include narrowing the target population to where positivity is supported, revising the treatment strategy to one whose counterfactual is identifiable from the data, changing the follow-up window, switching from a marginal to a matched or overlap-restricted target, or changing the missingness strategy. Each of these is an estimand revision, recorded in the analysis lock and decision log alongside the estimator changes that prompted it. Reporting the revised estimand transparently is preferable to reporting the original estimand with a documented override.

7.4 Threat-to-assumption matrix: what each scenario probes (and what it does not)

Each DQ scenario is best understood as an engineering approximation to a class of threats rather than an assumption-specific diagnostic. Table 4 makes that distinction explicit: for each scenario it lists the identification or measurement assumption nominally probed, the scenario operationalisation, and the threats the scenario does not probe. The table is a guide to interpreting stress_test() output; the five scenarios do not constitute a complete threat taxonomy.

A consequence is that the stress_test() output is useful for robustness screening of candidate estimators against prespecified threat ranges, not for validating the data source. Variable validation, source-data audit, and post-outcome quantitative bias analysis (Lash et al. 2014) remain separate activities, anchored in the validation literature (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b, 2021; European Medicines Agency 2026) and outside the simulation engine.

7.5 Calibration of severity ranges from external evidence

The DQ stress test is only as informative as the severity grids the analyst supplies. Each grid should be anchored in external evidence, not chosen for convenience:

  • Covariate missingness fractions should be calibrated to the observed missingness in the data source under study, plus realistic alternative scenarios from data-profiling studies (Kahn et al. 2016; U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b; European Medicines Agency 2026).
  • Treatment-ascertainment (sensitivity, specificity) ranges should come from claims-validation studies for the relevant exposure phenotype or from independent chart review (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a, 2024b).
  • Outcome-ascertainment (sensitivity, specificity) ranges should come from algorithm-validation studies or PPV / sensitivity literature for the outcome phenotype, with optional per-arm differential misclassification when the validation literature supports it (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a).
  • Unmeasured-confounder strengths (\(p_U\), \(\text{OR}_A\), \(\text{OR}_Y\)) should be elicited from subject-matter experts, prior-literature E-value bounds (VanderWeele and Ding 2017), or causal-gap sensitivity ranges (Dı́az and Laan 2013).

We recommend that the analyst record, in the decision log, a brief citation for each severity range alongside the lock fingerprint, so that a reviewer can check both the values and their provenance. The boundaries of what this screen does not establish (data-source validation, causal identification, post-outcome sensitivity, and independent governance) are listed concisely in the regulatory alignment table (Section 2, Table 15) and in the limitations paragraph in the Discussion (Section 13).

8 A quantitative supplement to fit-for-purpose review

This section describes how the pre-outcome decision is currently scored in published TL-RWE pipelines and what changes when the DQ stress test feeds into the same decision. The test scores robustness of candidate estimators against prespecified threat ranges; the validity of those ranges, and of the data source itself, remains an external study-level argument anchored in source-specific assessment guidance (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a, 2024b; European Medicines Agency 2026) (see Table 15).

A note on terminology: Muntner et al. (2024) describe three review-team decisions (“proceed to the next stage”, “conduct additional analyses to address bias”, or “terminate the study”), which we abbreviate in the decision-rule analyses of this manuscript as GO, FLAG, and STOP. GO means proceed to the locked primary analysis; FLAG means proceed only with documented review or qualification; STOP means do not conduct or report the primary comparative analysis under the current estimand, design, and specification. The mapping to the Muntner et al. wording is one-to-one; these are shorthand for their recommendations, not additional machinery. The support verdicts of Section 6 (PASS, FLAG, SEVERE, FAIL) grade a diagnostic, not a decision, and feed the decision through the declared ladder trigger.

8.1 What the pre-outcome decision currently does

In the published TL-RWE literature the pre-outcome decision is a prespecified set of qualitative checks: the SAP exists, the lock is in place, the cohort meets minimum size and event criteria, the propensity-score overlap looks acceptable, and the negative- control-outcome estimate is consistent with no effect (Dang et al. 2023; Gruber, Lee, et al. 2024; Gruber, Phillips, Lee, Concato, et al. 2024). Each check is binary or ordinal, and each is computed from a different source (a PDF SAP, a balance table, a negative-control estimate). When the data-fitness argument is added, it usually appears as a separate document (the SPIFD2 or HARPER table (Wang, Sreedhara, and Schneeweiss 2023)) and is adjudicated by reviewers rather than scored against the prespecified decision rule.

8.2 What the DQ supplement adds

The DQ stress test reports, for each candidate, the same triple (bias, RMSE, coverage) at each severity of each threat that the baseline plasmode reports. Because the units match, the same prespecified thresholds (maximum allowed bias, minimum allowed coverage, and an allowed SE-calibration window) can be applied uniformly to the baseline plasmode and to the degraded runs. The prespecified candidate is required to meet those thresholds both under the locked data-generating process and across the plausible range of each threat documented in the fit-for-purpose review. The thresholds are declared on the lock as dq_thresholds: a maximum absolute bias on the risk-difference scale, a minimum coverage, and a maximum RMSE ratio relative to the candidate’s own clean-data baseline, with optional FLAG levels for the last two. The package ships no default, because the values belong to the study: analysts should set them from the estimand magnitude, the prespecified Type I error budget, and the operating characteristics required by the receiver of the evidence, before the analysis lock is signed. The simulation of Section 10 declares a bias bound of 0.02 and the case study one of 0.01, both with a coverage floor of 0.90. The lock fingerprints the declared values, and the verdict and tipping points that stress_test() reports are pure functions of those values, the declared threat grid, and the computed metrics, so there is no reading-time judgment for the realised effect to steer.

This shifts the pre-outcome decision in three ways. First, the data-fitness argument becomes numeric and candidate-specific: instead of a prose claim that “the outcome ascertainment algorithm has reported sensitivity 0.90,” the analyst sees that at sensitivity = 0.90 and specificity = 0.95 the bias of the selected candidate rises from near zero to 0.004, still within the prespecified threshold of 0.010. The steeper threat is unmeasured confounding: at OR\(_A\) = OR\(_Y\) = 2.0 the same candidate’s bias reaches 0.010, touching the threshold, and RMSE rises by 9 % relative to the baseline plasmode. Second, the default select_candidate() rule, which picks the RMSE-minimiser on the baseline plasmode, gains the option rule = "min_max_rmse", which selects the candidate with the lowest worst-case RMSE across the DQ scenarios; a candidate that wins on the baseline but collapses under a positivity violation loses to a slightly less efficient one that maintains acceptable performance across the entire plausible range. Section 10.4 exhibits a candidate grid under which this rule changes the locked estimator. Third, because the baseline plasmode and the stressed runs are one stress_test() object that carries the locked thresholds and the declared grid, and the design log records their declaration, a reviewer can see the externally derived ranges that went in, the prespecified thresholds that came out, and reproduce the decision.

8.3 Position relative to other bias analyses

The DQ stress test is distinct from quantitative bias analysis (QBA) (Lash et al. 2014) and from the targeted-learning causal-gap sensitivity analysis of Dı́az and Laan (2013). QBA adjusts the final effect estimate for a postulated bias and is an unblinding-stage tool; causal-gap characterises how the estimate changes as a function of an unmeasured-confounder bound and complements the E-value (VanderWeele and Ding 2017). The DQ stress test, by contrast, asks whether candidate estimators still pass the pre-outcome decision when the data are degraded under prespecified threats, and reaches covariate missingness and exposure misclassification in particular.

We therefore position the DQ stress test as the first of three sequential bias analyses: pre-outcome (DQ stress test), at-outcome (negative-control outcomes (Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen, and Cohen 2010)), and post-outcome (E-value, QBA, causal-gap). Each addresses a different threat, at a different stage, with a different output.

8.4 Why “outcome-blind” matters here

The plasmode generator and DQ stress test use all the data except the outcome: real baseline covariates \(W\), real treatment assignment \(A\), real missingness indicators, real follow-up intervals, but not the observed primary treatment-outcome association. This phrasing, which we adopt from the FIORD outcome-blind simulation literature (Nance et al. 2026), states the admissibility condition directly. Every input to the candidate evaluation is drawn from the study data except the comparative quantity the analysis is supposed to estimate.
