11 Operating characteristics of the pre-outcome gate

The simulation in Section 10 shows the workflow returning the prespecified staged verdict in three scenarios, but it does not measure the screen as a decision rule. A reviewer is entitled to ask how often the gate’s verdict agrees with the verdict an oracle would reach knowing the realised estimator’s true bias, and how that agreement degrades when the simulated-outcome model is misspecified. We answer this with a calibration meta-simulation (run_gate_operating_characteristics.R in the companion repository).

The design isolates the unmeasured-confounding threat. For a grid of true confounder strengths \(s\) (odds ratios on both treatment and outcome), we compute two quantities at each \(s\). The oracle bias \(B_{\text{real}}(s)\) is the mean bias of the realised TMLE, adjusting for the measured covariates only, when a true unmeasured confounder of strength \(s\) acts on both the treatment and the outcome. The screen-predicted bias \(B_{\text{screen}}(s)\) is what the outcome-blind plasmode screen anticipates at the same strength: the treatment and outcome nuisance surfaces \(g_0(W)\) and \(Q_0(W)\) are fitted on the analyst’s cohort, a what-if confounder of strength \(s\) is injected into both the simulated treatment and the simulated outcome, and the same TMLE is scored against the simulated truth. The simulated nuisances are fitted two ways, a misspecified GLM and a flexible SuperLearner (GLM, MARS, and random forest), under both a linear and a nonlinear true surface, and the locked STOP threshold is applied to both the oracle and the screen. The realised estimator uses a GLM nuisance library, so that under the nonlinear surface its bias reflects nuisance misspecification as well as the omitted confounder, and the screen can predict that bias only if its simulated nuisances reproduce the nonlinearity.

Against the oracle, over all 10 cells the screen with a flexible (SuperLearner) simulated-nuisance model attains sensitivity 1.00 and specificity 1.00; with a GLM simulated-nuisance model these are 0.62 and 1.00. The whole gap is on the nonlinear surface: the GLM screen’s sensitivity is 1.00 on the linear surface but falls to 0.40 on the nonlinear surface, whereas the flexible screen holds sensitivity 1.00 there. That difference quantifies the cost of misspecifying the simulated-nuisance model, the central plasmode pitfall (Schreck et al. 2024).

Two patterns bound what the screen can and cannot predict. First, the screen predicts the realised bias well only to the extent that the analyst names a confounder of the right strength: it calibrates against threats of the specified magnitude, but a true confounder stronger than anticipated is not detected, so a STOP is evidence of fragility while a GO is not a certificate of robustness (Section 8.5). Second, under a nonlinear true surface the GLM screen under-predicts the realised bias, because its simulated treatment and outcome surfaces are too simple to reproduce the nuisance misspecification that biases the realised estimator, whereas the flexible screen reproduces it and tracks the oracle more closely. This is the reason the package exposes a q0_library argument and why we recommend a flexible simulated-nuisance model. Two limitations of this grid temper the reported numbers. The specificity of 1.00 rests on only the two GO cells in the sweep, both on the linear surface (the nonlinear surface contains no GO cell), so the screen’s false-STOP behaviour on a nonlinear surface is untested. And on the nonlinear surface the gate is flagging nuisance misspecification, not only unmeasured confounding: at the no-confounder cell (\(s = 1\), OR \(= 1\)) the realised bias is already about 0.07 and the cell STOPs, so the nonlinear sensitivity measures the screen’s detection of GLM misspecification as much as of the latent confounder. The two failure modes coincide here by construction, and a wider grid with more GO cells and a confounder-free nonlinear baseline would be needed to separate them. These operating characteristics come from the final 200-replicate run reported in Table 7; the per-cell bias estimates carry Monte Carlo standard errors on the order of 0.001 to 0.002, well inside the margins that separate each STOP verdict from the locked threshold.

12 Case Study: Rescue.Co Kenya Trauma Registry

12.1 Why a real-data workflow demonstration

We use the Rescue.Co Kenya Trauma Registry as a real comparative-effectiveness study that exercises the full workflow on genuine registry data, while presenting the resulting estimates as an illustration; they are not confirmatory evidence about the causal effect of Rescue.Co transport. The simulation in Section 10 is small (5 covariates, n = 2,000, fully observed outcome) by design, so that each threat can be controlled analytically. A working framework also has to execute on real observational data: covariates drawn from multiple instruments, outcomes missing for non-trivial fractions of the cohort, and confounders the protocol did not anticipate. The registry is an applied comparative-effectiveness study at three Nairobi hospitals (KNH, Mama Lucy, Mbagathi) comparing prehospital transport by a specialised emergency-medical-services provider (Rescue.Co) with other modes of arrival, on six-month mortality, functional outcome, and care-process timing. The case study analyses five prespecified transport contrasts on the 8,323 patients with known transport mode, each under its own lock on the shared cohort, and its central finding is about estimability rather than about any single effect: the protocol’s primary comparison places two-fifths of the sample outside the propensity band, the design stage grades it severe, and the pre-registered ladder re-targets the analysis before any outcome is joined. All stages were run on cleanTMLE 0.2.0, with the package version and the lock fingerprints recorded in the released case-study metadata, and the analysis code is available in the companion repository. The individual-level registry data are access-restricted (see the ethics and data-availability statement below), so the case study can be reproduced from its code but not from public data. The DQ stress test reported in Section 12.6 comes from the earlier single-contrast run at 50 replicates, an illustration below the 200-replicate bar used for inferential interpretation; the support maps and design comparison of Section 12.3 run at 200 replicates. The example illustrates a real-registry execution of the workflow and is not primary evidence of DQ-stress validity, which the simulation in Section 10 provides.

Ethics and data availability. The Rescue.Co Kenya Trauma Registry is a real, IRB-governed dataset of human trauma patients. The study was approved by [approving ethics committee and approval number to be completed], and participation was covered by [informed consent / an approved waiver of consent to be completed]. Because the registry contains identifiable and sensitive individual-level information (including HIV/ART status and socioeconomic indicators), the patient-level data cannot be shared publicly and are not included in the companion repository; the rescueCo/ data and result files are excluded from version control for this reason. The analysis code, the analysis-lock fingerprint, and aggregate outputs are available in the companion repository, and de-identified individual-level data are available from the authors on reasonable request, subject to the governing data-use agreement and ethics approval.

The example is interesting for five reasons that the simulation does not exercise: (a) the protocol’s primary comparison has a severe practical positivity violation, so the estimability machinery of Section 6 carries the analysis; (b) the functional outcome (Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended, GOSE 1–8) (Wilson, Pettigrew, and Teasdale 1998) is missing for a quarter of the cohort from loss to 6-month follow-up; (c) inter-facility transfers and patients with prior care are unevenly distributed across arms, and the pre-registered exclusions that remove them turn out to carry the measurable confounding; (d) an 8-week healthcare-worker strike (15 March 2024 to 8 May 2024) acts as a quasi-natural-experiment confounder that is not part of either SPIFD2 or the five threats encoded by stress_test(); and (e) five prespecified negative controls, two socioeconomic and three chronic-condition, screen for residual confounding, with two of them too rare to estimate and labelled as such instead of dropped silently (Conover et al. 2025).

12.2 Contrasts, outcomes, and pre-specification

The study cohort is the 8,323 registry patients with known transport mode. Five contrasts are prespecified, each with its own analysis lock built by create_contrast_locks() on the shared cohort (Table 8): the protocol’s primary comparison C1 (Rescue.Co against everyone else), C2 (Rescue.Co against non-ambulance arrival), C3 (any ambulance against non-ambulance), C4 (Rescue.Co against other ambulance, transfers included), and the PRIMARY cohort contrast (Rescue.Co against other ambulance with inter-facility transfers and prior-care patients excluded, the cohort the study’s earlier single-contrast demonstration analysed). The presented outcomes are six-month mortality (death_by_6mo, the primary) and time to ambulance arrival in minutes, the outcome whose extrapolated estimate motivates the Introduction; severe disability (GOSE \(\le\) 4, so the rare category is the event) and the remaining registry outcomes run through the same locks. Missing follow-up is handled by IPCW as the primary missingness path with complete case as the sensitivity. The outcome columns are physically absent from the design stage: the locks carry masked placeholders, and the outcome store is joined only at estimation.

Each lock declares the same estimand ladder before outcome access: ATE as the primary, then trimmed ATE, ATT, and ATO as ordered fallbacks, with a SEVERE support verdict as the switching trigger and a matched ATT carried as a sensitivity analysis. Ninety design columns survive the sanitize_covariates() near-zero-variance and aliasing filters, covering demographics, injury place, mechanism and intent, severity (GCS, ISS components), distance, payment, SES proxies, the chronic-condition panel, and calendar time. The propensity library is the build_sl_library() “rwe_wide” preset (penalised logistic learners, PCA-reduced GLMs, and the marginal mean; no tree learners, which can separate arms on wide indicator designs), with \(V = 10\) following Phillips et al. (2023). Five negative controls are registered on every lock, tagged with their Muntner et al. (2024) confounding domains: urban household and wood-or-charcoal cooking fuel (health-seeking behaviour, access to care), and hypertension, insulin-treated diabetes, and HIV on ART (confounding by indication, functional status). Care-process indicators (vitals missingness, examination markers) are registered for the collider check and excluded from the adjustment set.

12.3 The design stage: support and estimand feasibility

Table 9 shows the support assessment per contrast, computed by assess_support() on each lock’s fitted propensity.

The protocol comparison C1 places 40.6% of the sample outside the band with a maximum ATE weight of 257, and C2 is nearly as bad; both are graded SEVERE, which is the declared ladder trigger. The violation is not a thin tail. The tree search localises it to interpretable regions: patients injured at home (1,386 patients, 1.4% treated), other non-street injury places, and assault victims outside those places (4.2% treated). These patients essentially never receive Rescue.Co transport, so the counterfactual “everyone transported by Rescue.Co” is unanswerable for them without extrapolation. C3 and C4 are graded FLAG, and the PRIMARY cohort contrast passes (0.06% outside, maximum weight 8): restricting to ambulance arrivals without transfers or prior care removes the never-treated strata, at the cost of a narrower question.

The per-estimand feasibility table then reads each fitted propensity per estimand. On C1 the ATE is infeasible, while the ATT bounds its control weights at 5.0 (the largest treated propensity is 0.85), the ATO bounds all weights at 1 by construction, and the trimmed ATE retains 4,946 patients after removing 3,377, nearly all controls. The removal profile makes the estimand change concrete: the removed patients are far more often injured at home (40% versus 1% of the retained, standardised difference 1.10) or in assaults (39% versus 10%), are younger, live farther away, and more often sought prior care. A trimmed analysis of C1 is not about those patients, and the design report says so in words (Crump et al. 2009).

12.3.1 The outcome-blind support map

simulate_support() ran 200 generate-treatment replicates per contrast over the prespecified surface family (simulated confounding strength 0, 1, 2 along the separating direction, crossed with effect modification off and on) and scored each estimand’s estimator against a bias tolerance of 0.01 at a coverage floor of 0.90. Two readings of the resulting map matter, and they answer different questions.

On C1 the map corroborates the static verdict from an independent direction: the ATE fails at the mildest surface (coverage 0.87 while the bounded estimands sit at 0.95), before any simulated confounding is added, which is the signature of a support failure rather than of the stress. The bounded estimands (ATT, ATO, matched ATT, and with one marginal cell the trimmed ATE) hold through the moderate surfaces and degrade only at the harshest rung. On the PRIMARY contrast every estimand passes the mildest surface, and as the simulated confounding strengthens the unmatched estimands degrade together (coverage 0.81 to 0.89 at the harshest rung) while the matched ATT holds 0.93 to 0.96 throughout; degradation that arrives only with the stress, and hits all weighting-based estimands alike, reads as confounding-strength stress; a positivity problem would have shown at the mildest surface, and the PASS verdict says there is none. These two patterns are the map’s value: it separates “fails because the design lacks support” (C1’s ATE, failing at baseline) from “fails because the stress is harsh” (the harshest rung everywhere). A summary rule that requires a whole-grid pass conflates the two, and on these data would keep only the matched ATT; the design reports therefore read the map over the moderate-confounding region for the support question and report the whole-grid result as a conservative bound, a reading rule recorded in the design log before estimation.

12.3.2 Generate-treatment versus sample-treatment on real data

The C1 lock also reruns its support simulation under the legacy sample-treatment design, holding everything else fixed, as a real-data check of the Shaw et al. (2025) argument (Table 10). At the mild surface the two designs agree. At the stressed surface the sample-treatment design, which carries the observed 41% violation into every replicate, inflates the bias of every bounded estimand by roughly half again (ATT 0.018 versus 0.013, ATO 0.016 versus 0.010) and collapses their coverage (ATT 0.69 versus 0.78, ATO 0.64 versus 0.79, matched ATT 0.63 versus 0.86), while the ATE’s RMSE balloons more than fivefold (0.066 versus 0.012) as the replicated violation meets the stressed surface. A support map built on the sample-treatment design would therefore have declared every estimand infeasible on C1, not because the design cannot support them but because the simulation manufactured the failure it was asked to detect.

12.4 Negative-control ladder and the collider check

The negative-control ladder fits all five registered controls, unadjusted, on each nested cohort: the full contrast cohort, then transfers excluded, then transfers and prior care excluded. On the full C4 cohort the two socioeconomic controls fail decisively (urban household +0.068, 95% CI 0.049 to 0.086; wood-or-charcoal fuel $-$0.052, CI $-$0.074 to $-$0.029): ambulance transfer patients differ socioeconomically from direct arrivals. Both turn null after the transfer exclusion (urban household +0.001) and stay null after the prior-care exclusion, and on the PRIMARY cohort every estimable control is null. On C1 the urban-household control fails on the full cohort (+0.013, CI 0.003 to 0.024) and has no restriction rung that repairs it, which corroborates the support verdict from an independent direction. Hypertension is null everywhere, and the two rare chronic controls (insulin-treated diabetes, HIV on ART) are labelled inestimable on every rung, following the Conover et al. (2025) practice of reporting inestimability rather than silently shrinking the panel. The reading is the study’s second methodological point: the pre-registered exclusions, not covariate adjustment, removed the measurable confounding, and the ladder shows which restriction did the work. A TMLE-adjusted variant of the same ladder is reported in the supplement with a caveat: on the restricted rungs it conditions on design columns that are near-copies of the socioeconomic controls, so its restricted-rung rows are not comparable to the unadjusted ladder.

The collider check regresses each care-process indicator on treatment given severity. Vitals-recorded-within-an-hour and blood-pressure-missingness are predicted by treatment on C3, C4, and the PRIMARY contrast (standardised differences 0.11 to 0.34), which is expected: transport mode changes the care process. The check confirms these variables belong outside the adjustment set, where the locks placed them; conditioning on them would open collider paths through in-hospital care.

12.5 Pre-outcome decision

design_report() assembles, per contrast, the support verdict, the feasibility table, the support map, the negative-control ladder, and the collider check, and closes with the recommendation the review team reads. For the PRIMARY contrast the recommendation is to proceed. For C1 and C2 it is to proceed with qualification: the declared primary (ATE) is not supported, the ladder moves to the trimmed ATE, then ATT, then ATO, and the switch is logged as a design decision with the SEVERE verdict as its recorded trigger. For C3 and C4 the recommendation is to proceed with the FLAG caveat attached. Every recommendation was fixed, and the design log exported, before the outcome store was joined.

12.6 Candidate selection and the DQ stress test

Candidate selection and the data-quality stress test were run on the PRIMARY cohort’s earlier single-contrast lock (functional outcome, four TMLE candidates varying the propensity library and truncation: glm_t01, glmnet_t01, ensemble_t01, ensemble_t05), and we report them from that run; the multi-arm rebuild reuses the locked candidate. The Stage 2b feasibility plasmode metrics on the locked DGP are:

Stage 2b feasibility plasmode metrics (rescueCo lock, 50 replicates per candidate, additive risk-difference effect of 0.05). On the clean-data baseline the four candidates are nearly tied (RMSE within 0.0002), so the min_rmse rule would pick glm_t01; under the five-threat DQ sweep they separate, and the minimax rule picks ensemble_t05 instead.
Candidate Bias RMSE Coverage
glm_t01 +0.00001 0.0134 0.92
ensemble_t05 +0.00076 0.0135 0.92
glmnet_t01 +0.00019 0.0135 0.92
ensemble_t01 +0.00082 0.0136 0.92

All four candidates pass the prespecified decision targets (max_abs_bias = 0.01, min_coverage = 0.90) on the clean-data baseline, where their performance is nearly indistinguishable because the propensity scores stay well inside the [0.01, 0.99] bounds (range 0.21–0.81). Under the prespecified five-threat DQ sweep, the worst-case RMSE ratio relative to baseline is 1.82 for glm_t01, 1.73 for glmnet_t01, 1.53 for ensemble_t01, and 1.27 for ensemble_t05; the largest contributor for each candidate is the near-positivity threat at slope \(\times 4\). The minimax rule therefore locks ensemble_t05 (the heaviest truncation), while a baseline-only rule would have locked glm_t01 (the lowest baseline RMSE, but also the most fragile candidate under stress). This makes the case study a real-data instance of the divergence reported in Section 10.4 on a constructed grid.

All four candidates passed the prespecified operating targets on the well-overlapped PRIMARY cohort, where their baseline performance is nearly indistinguishable. The Stage 2c DQ stress test sweeps the prespecified five-threat grid (near-positivity, covariate missingness under MCAR/MAR/MNAR, treatment and outcome misclassification, and unmeasured confounding) over the candidate grid, and the minimax rule locks ensemble_t05 as the primary specification. This is itself a divergence: the min_rmse rule would pick glm_t01 (the lowest baseline RMSE, 0.0134), but under the stress sweep glm_t01 has the highest worst-case RMSE ratio (1.82, driven by the near-positivity threat), while ensemble_t05 (which uses heavier truncation and a small ensemble library) has the lowest (1.27). The case study therefore reproduces, on a real-data lock, the same mechanism that the constructed divergence study in Section 10.4 demonstrates: a candidate selected for clean-data efficiency is the most exposed under the prespecified threat sweep, and the minimax rule reroutes the selection toward a more robust specification. The reported result uses a 50-replicate run (rescueCo/scripts/rescueco_dq_full.R, see Section 15), an illustration below the 200-replicate bar we adopt for inferential interpretation, consistent with the case study being a workflow demonstration rather than confirmatory evidence; a 200-replicate confirmation is the analyst’s next step for a submission-grade analysis. The 3-replicate configuration bundled with the staged pipeline is a continuous-integration smoke test and is not used for inference.

12.7 Effect estimates

Estimation runs only after the design reports above are fixed. run_estimand_ladder() executes per lock and outcome: the declared primary (ATE) where the trigger was not met, and the feasible fallbacks (trimmed ATE, ATT, ATO, with the matched ATT as sensitivity) where it was. Each row carries its estimand label, the lock’s support verdict, and the implausibility flags, and the design log records the C1 and C2 switches with the SEVERE verdict as their trigger. Table 11 shows the six-month mortality rows.

The substantive pattern is coherent across the ladder. The within-ambulance contrasts favour Rescue.Co on six-month mortality: the C4 primary row is \(-2.9\) percentage points (95% CI \(-4.9\) to \(-0.9\)), and on the primary cohort the effect concentrates among the treated (ATT \(-2.8\), CI \(-4.8\) to \(-0.9\); ATE \(-1.7\), CI \(-3.5\) to \(0.1\)), with the overlap-weighted rows nearest the null. The against-everyone contrasts C1 and C2 are null on every feasible estimand. C3, any ambulance against non-ambulance arrival, shows higher mortality (+1.8 points, CI 0.8 to 2.8), and the design stage supplies its reading: both socioeconomic negative controls fail on that contrast with no pre-registered restriction that repairs them, and its care-process indicators are treatment-predicted, so the design report carries C3 as residually confounded by indication rather than as a harm signal. On time to arrival, the population contrasts agree that ambulances, and Rescue.Co in particular, reach patients three to four and a half hours sooner (for example C3 \(-245\) minutes, CI \(-320\) to \(-169\)); the transfers-included C4 gap of \(-100\) to \(-205\) minutes shrinks to a null \(-0.1\) minutes (CI \(-32\) to \(31\)) on the primary cohort, so the gap is carried by the transfer and prior-care strata that the primary cohort excludes. No row anywhere tripped the implausibility guard.

Two readings of this table concern the workflow itself. First, the severe-overlap contrasts do not answer the protocol’s original question. C2 carries no ATE row at all; C1 carries exactly one, estimated under a logged override whose recorded reason is reconciliation (the parallel unblinded pipeline reports the C1 ATE as a SEVERE-flagged diagnostic, and the row lets the two pipelines be compared), and it arrives wearing its SEVERE label with a standard error several times larger than the bounded rows beside it. The substantive C1 and C2 answers are the trimmed, treated-population and overlap-weighted effects, each labelled with the population it is about. What a conventional pipeline would have reported for C1, an IPTW or TMLE ATE under weights reaching 257 and no label, is exactly the kind of estimate the Introduction’s motivating failure warns about, and the same ladder run re-analyses that failure’s own outcome: time to arrival, where an earlier full-cohort analysis produced +14,637 minutes against a crude difference of seven hours in the other direction, is estimated here only through bounded-weight estimands, with the implausibility guard comparing every row against the bounds the raw arm summaries impose. Second, the estimates that are reported agree with the parallel unblinded main analysis of the same registry where the two pipelines are comparable; the matched ATT on the functional dichotomy differs from the main pipeline’s estimate by well under a quarter of a standard error, and the reconciliation table released with the case study tracks every (contrast, outcome, estimand, estimator) pair across the two pipelines. Per-row E-values (VanderWeele and Ding 2017) via compute_evalue() and outcome-missingness delta sensitivity via run_delta_sensitivity() accompany the primary rows in the released files. The healthcare-worker strike period remains an unmodelled threat that the prespecified threat families do not cover, and we carry it as an unquantified limitation.

12.8 What the case study tells us about the workflow

12.8.1 Prespecification, the design log, and an honest failure

The design log captured every prespecified analytic choice (the contrast definitions, the exclusions, the ladder declarations, the truncation and threshold settings) with timestamps, and the lock fingerprints reconciled on every reload. The most instructive record, though, is a failure from the study’s earlier single-contrast run. That run’s primary outcome was the good-outcome dichotomy of GOSE, with prevalence 0.92, so the rare category carried too few events; the cohort-adequacy checkpoint recorded STOP, and the pipeline proceeded anyway through an unlogged override, a tryCatch around the authorisation check with nothing recorded between the STOP and the estimate. The September reconciliation against the parallel unblinded analysis surfaced this because the earlier version’s audit trail had preserved both records: the STOP and the estimate, with no rationale between them. The rebuild fixed the design rather than the log: the outcome set was aligned to the main analysis (mortality as primary, severe disability as the functional dichotomy, so the rare category is the event), and overrides now require a logged reason, so the record can no longer show STOP followed silently by estimation. We report this because it is the working theory of the framework in miniature: the value of the record is that it makes such gaps findable, including gaps in the workflow’s own conduct.

12.8.2 Outcome-blind plasmode

Stage 2b feasibility coverage of 0.94 with bias below 0.001 across 50 replicates is the kind of design validation a reviewer would want, and the 200-replicate support maps of Section 12.3 extend the same device to the estimability question. Stage 2c then runs the full DQ stress test (stress_test()) over the prespecified threat sweep and produces a structural pass on each scenario at 50 replicates per threat-severity cell (an illustration below the 200-replicate inferential bar; see Section 15 for the entry point). The five threats encoded by stress_test() (covariate missingness under MCAR/MAR/MNAR, exposure misclassification, outcome misclassification, latent \(U\), and near-positivity) still do not cover one design challenge that mattered in the rescueCo study, the strike-window confounder, which motivates the time-window extension in Section 13.6.

12.8.3 Simulated-outcome fidelity

The plasmode resamples the empirical covariate structure of the rescueCo cohort, redraws treatment from the fitted propensity (Section 6.4), and generates simulated outcomes from a covariate-only model \(Q_0(W) = E[Y \mid W]\), so the simulated covariate marginals match the observed ones by construction. Because a logistic \(Q_0\) with an intercept forces the fitted mean to equal the observed mean, a marginal prevalence match is automatic and is not by itself evidence of fidelity, so we assess \(Q_0\) out of sample instead. Fitting \(Q_0(W)\) on the earlier run’s complete-case functional-outcome cohort (\(n = 1277\), outcome prevalence 0.904) and evaluating it by ten-fold cross-validation, the covariate-only outcome model discriminates the observed outcome with a cross-validated AUC of 0.64 (the in-sample AUC of 0.72 is optimistic by resubstitution), and its out-of-sample calibration has a maximum absolute predicted-minus-observed deviation across risk deciles of 0.061. This establishes that the plasmode preserves the covariate structure and a moderately discriminating, reasonably calibrated marginal outcome model, not that it reproduces the joint treatment-outcome law. The simulated outcome carries a fixed risk difference and no effect modification, and the fidelity of that joint structure to the realised process cannot be checked before the outcome is unblinded, so the diagnostic is necessary for fidelity without being sufficient, consistent with the limitation in Section 13.

12.8.4 Estimator functions and real-data robustness

Applying cleanTMLE 0.1.0 to the original rescueCo lock surfaced more than a dozen distinct issues, six of them blocking, which the 0.1.x releases addressed: stress_test() failed outright on a lock with NA in the outcome (now guarded), the step-by-step TMLE functions refused to fit on NA outcomes (now subset to complete cases with an MCAR warning), the SuperLearner propensity fit crashed on stale parallel backends (now sequential by default), and failed negative-control fits were dropped silently (now recorded). The multi-arm rebuild then drove the 0.2.0 redesign in the other direction: the support assessment, the per-estimand feasibility reading, the estimand ladder, and the generate-treatment plasmode all exist because this study needed them, and the same rebuild consolidated the exported surface from 149 functions to 54 after the governance layer grew faster than its evidential value. The September 2026 revision (0.3.0) went further in the same direction: the workflow surface is sixteen verbs, the checkpoint and authorisation-token layer is deleted, the primary outcome lives in a store the lock’s data frame never holds, and the decision rules the verdicts read are declared and fingerprinted at lock creation. We document both directions because the working theory of the framework is that the prespecification record should make problems visible, including problems with the package itself, instead of absorbing them into a hand-edited final table.

The full release notes are in cleanTMLE/NEWS.md, and the case study’s results/multiarm/ directory contains the CSV files behind every table in this section, together with the reconciliation table against the parallel unblinded analysis.

13 Discussion

13.1 What cleanTMLE contributes operationally

The novelty in this paper is not causal identification. The roadmap and target-trial literature (Dang et al. 2023; Petersen and Laan 2014; M. A. Hernán and Robins 2016) already provides that frame, and the package operates inside its estimation and pre-outcome diagnostics steps. The novelty is that two questions usually settled informally become explicit, prespecified outputs of the blind phase. The first is estimability: the support assessment, the per-estimand feasibility reading, the outcome-blind support map, and the estimand ladder together answer “is this comparison estimable, and with which estimand” before the outcome is examined, and convert any estimand switch into a logged design decision. The second is robustness: the DQ stress test adds a candidate-specific pre-outcome screen on top of the standard plasmode loop. Around both, the analysis-lock object and the design log make the prespecification a reproducible record, supporting transparent reconstruction of paper-only prespecification checklists (Gruber, Lee, et al. 2024; Cashin et al. 2024) by an external reviewer.

The contribution is operational, and a useful test is to ask what evidence the package can and cannot produce. cleanTMLE can document that the analyst prespecified the estimand ladder, the candidate estimators, the decision thresholds, and the severity ranges; that the support and feasibility verdicts, and any estimand switch, were fixed before unblinding; that the locked candidate was the one that ran on the real outcome; and that a fingerprinted record captures the sequence. cleanTMLE cannot demonstrate that the data source is fit for the regulatory question, that the exposure or outcome phenotypes have been validated, that the target population is the regulatory decision population, or that the unmeasured-confounder bound is defensible. Nor can the support machinery see past the measured covariates: a propensity model that misses the separating covariate will not warn, which is why the negative-control ladder and the stratum checks run beside the global statistics. Those remain study-level activities, anchored in target-trial protocols (M. A. Hernán and Robins 2016; Cashin et al. 2024), source-specific guidance (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a, 2024b, 2021; European Medicines Agency 2024, 2026), and post-outcome sensitivity analyses (VanderWeele and Ding 2017; Lash et al. 2014; Dı́az and Laan 2013).

13.2 How the workflow aligns with regulatory expectations

For high-stakes regulatory or confirmatory RWE, cleanTMLE is best used as one layer in a broader governed workflow. The lock and the design log track the prespecification and traceability that FDA RWE program guidance, EMA RWD guidance, and the NICE RWE framework expect (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018, 2024a, 2024c; European Medicines Agency 2024; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence 2022) and match the data-quality dimensions in the EMA RWD framework (European Medicines Agency 2026) and ICH M14 (March 2026) (International Council for Harmonisation 2026), as summarised in Table 15. As stated in the abstract, the software layer sits inside, rather than substitutes for, the personnel-based governance this guidance requires: documented source assessment, role-based access controls, and structured protocol records.

13.3 Comparison with adjacent tools

Table 12 places cleanTMLE against the nearest alternatives, to make explicit which capabilities are shared and which are specific to the package. The combination that distinguishes cleanTMLE is the design-stage estimability answer (support assessment, per-estimand feasibility, the support map, and the estimand ladder), the outcome-blind plasmode candidate selection with the DQ stress test on the same decision scale, and the prespecification record (lock and design log), bound to a doubly robust estimator layer that reproduces a mature cumulative-risk package (Section 12, and the side-by-side ACTG 320 reproduction in the companion repository).

The contrast with the E-value is treated once in Section 10.5, where the post-hoc E-value and the pre-hoc, candidate-specific DQ stress test are shown to answer different questions and to be worth reporting together.

Quantitative bias analysis (Lash et al. 2014) adjusts the final estimate for postulated biases. Like the E-value, QBA is an unblinding-stage tool. The DQ stress test does not adjust the estimate; it asks whether the estimator continues to meet the prespecified performance criteria when the biases are present. We therefore recommend QBA at the analysis stage and the DQ stress test at the prespecification stage.

The targeted-learning causal-gap sensitivity analysis (Dı́az and Laan 2013) characterises the change in \(\Psi\) as the unmeasured-confounder bound varies. Causal-gap is unblinding-stage and characterises one threat (unmeasured confounding) in a TL- specific way. The DQ stress test is broader (it covers five threats) but cruder (it does not adjust the estimate). Both are useful and complementary.

Negative-control outcomes (Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen, and Cohen 2010) test for residual confounding in the realised data. Because they use real data, they are at-outcome rather than pre-outcome. The DQ stress test cannot detect residual confounding; the NCO check cannot detect covariate missingness or exposure misclassification. They target different threats. Muntner et al. (2024) recommend selecting NCOs across four domains (confounding by indication, functional status, health-seeking behaviour, and access to healthcare) and Levintow et al. (2023) give pragmatic guidance for choosing them; the cleanTMLE workflow records each declared NCO and its domain in the lock and the design log, so the chosen domains are part of the record.

Kent (2026) reports a worked applied use of the staging framework for a comparative-effectiveness study of evolocumab versus non-treatment for major adverse cardiovascular events in the Komodo Healthcare Map: negative-control outcomes flagged residual bias in the health-seeking-behaviour domain, the review team allowed the study to proceed conditional on a pre-specified E-value quantitative-bias-analysis plan, and the final risk difference at four years was reported as roughly \(-4\%\). The example illustrates both the staged decision rule and the role of negative-control domains in practice.

13.4 Limitations of plasmode data-quality stress testing

A plasmode data-quality stress test is only as informative as the simulated outcome model and degradation mechanisms used to generate it. Passing the pre-outcome decision rule does not establish identification, remove unmeasured confounding, validate the data source, or demonstrate that the target population matches the regulatory decision population. It shows only that, under the prespecified outcome-generating mechanism and degradation ranges, a candidate estimator maintained acceptable finite-sample performance according to the chosen criteria. Severity ranges should therefore be justified from external validation studies, data profiling, subject-matter knowledge, expert elicitation, or formal sensitivity-analysis bounds. When such evidence is weak, the stress test should be interpreted as exploratory rather than confirmatory.

The DQ stress test also depends on the same parametric simulated-outcome model used by the baseline plasmode. If that model misrepresents the joint covariate-treatment-outcome distribution (for example by omitting effect modification or mis-specifying functional form), the simulated bias and coverage under stressed scenarios may be optimistic or pessimistic in ways that no amount of replication can correct.

13.5 Other limitations

The current implementation has additional limitations the analyst should keep in mind, grouped into the candidate-selection rule, model assumptions, computational cost, and estimand scope.

13.5.1 Candidate-selection rule (FIORD alignment)

The FIORD outcome-blind simulation guidance (Nance et al. 2026) separates candidate selection into two tasks: first screen point estimators by oracle coverage (a CI built from the Monte Carlo empirical SE) and pick the lowest-variance survivor, then select the variance method on the locked point estimator using nominal CI coverage. cleanTMLE implements both stages. Stage one is select_candidate(rule = "fiord_two_stage"), which screens candidates to those within fiord_coverage_tol of nominal oracle coverage and locks in the lowest-SE survivor (the default rule = "min_rmse", optionally "min_max_rmse" over the DQ stress scenarios, remains available as a single-step alternative). Stage two is select_variance_method(), which, with the point estimator fixed, compares variance methods by their oracle coverage on simulated data and returns the one closest to nominal; bootstrap_rd_variance() supplies a native nonparametric bootstrap standard error and percentile interval for the marginal risk difference under TMLE or stabilised IPTW. The bootstrap is one option when the influence-function variance is suspect. For stabilised IPTW the influence-function variance treats the propensity score as known (J. M. Robins and Rotnitzky (1992)), and resampling does not remove that conservatism, so the bootstrap interval is reported alongside the influence-function interval and the better-calibrated one is chosen on oracle coverage. For a matched cohort the standard nonparametric bootstrap is not consistent (Abadie and Imbens (2008)), and the full-pipeline re-matching variant is reported as an empirical correction. The remaining limitation is practical. The variance-method stage is exposed as a separate call and is not folded into a single run_* wrapper, and the bootstrap multiplies computation, so analysts reserve it for the estimators where the IF variance is known to misbehave.

13.5.2 Model assumptions

The covariate-missingness scenario degrades \(W\) under MCAR, MAR, and MNAR masks, so the stress test can probe missingness that depends on observed covariates (MAR) or on the masked value itself (MNAR). The only missing-data handling exercised, however, is median imputation: the degraded covariate is filled with its column median before each candidate is refit. A principled alternative is inverse-probability-of-missingness weighting or multiple imputation, which under MAR recovers valid inference where median imputation does not; a native cleanTMLE implementation of that path is future work.

The plasmode DGP itself is parametric. The outcome is generated from a logistic regression of \(Y\) on \(W\) fitted to the lock data, and the simulated effect is constant on the risk-difference scale (\(p_1^{\text{sim}} = p_0^{\text{sim}} + \Delta\)). Effect modification, time-varying treatment, and competing risks would need a richer DGP. The package architecture permits these extensions; the simulation reported here does not exercise them. stress_test() takes a q0_library argument so the analyst can fit Q0 with a SuperLearner library in place of the default logistic GLM; this relaxes the bias of candidate selection toward linear-in-logit learners when the underlying outcome surface is nonlinear. A companion pilot simulation (plasmode_selection_paper/) provides the empirical motivation: at n = 500, a logistic-GLM Q0 produces no detectable separation between fixed-library and plasmode- selected TMLE workflows because both inherit the same linearity bias.

The plausible degradation ranges have to come from external evidence. The software cannot decide whether 5 % or 20 % covariate missingness is realistic for a given data source; the analyst has to cite a profiling or validation study. SPIFD2 makes the same demand qualitatively, and the DQ stress test inherits it.

13.5.3 PS candidate grid and learner stability

The DQ stress test generates simulated outcomes under degraded covariate, treatment, and confounder distributions, and then re-fits every candidate PS model on each simulated dataset. The simulated designs for Scenario B (marginal overlap, PS range 0.037–0.990) produced numerical instability in regularised learners: SL.glmnet ran away on computation with no convergence signal, inflating wall time by more than an order of magnitude relative to GLM. The simulation in Section 10 therefore uses a three-candidate GLM PS grid (\(t \in \{0.001, 0.025, 0.20\}\)) for the DQ stress test; SL.glmnet is retained in the SuperLearner library for the cross-fitted TMLE nuisance fits, where it operates on the full (undegraded) observed-data sample. In practice, the GLM and regularised-learner PS produce near-identical plasmode metrics on the simple logistic DGP used here, so the omission does not change the candidate-selection outcome. Analysts with more complex DGPs or learner libraries that include tree-based or spline models should profile DQ-stress runtime on a small representative run before committing to a full grid.

13.5.4 Computational cost

Each scenario \(\times\) severity cell adds a full set of plasmode replicates. With the configuration of Section 10 (30 plasmode replicates per cell, 19 degraded severity cells, and three PS candidates) the stress test fits about 1,700 candidate TMLE models per Monte Carlo scenario, or roughly 6,800 across the four scenarios, alongside the undegraded baseline plasmode. Each fit uses a GLM-nuisance TMLE, so a full per-scenario run, including the 200-replicate main Monte Carlo, completed in about twelve minutes on a current multi-core workstation in our runs, and the four-scenario study fits inside a conventional statistical-analysis-plan timeline. Larger candidate grids or higher replicate counts scale linearly; parallelising over severity cells is the most direct route for interactive use.

13.5.5 Estimand scope

The running estimands in this paper are marginal risk contrasts for a binary point exposure: the ATE and its trimmed version, the ATT, and the overlap-weighted ATO, all on the risk-difference scale, with multi-arm exposures handled as prespecified pairwise contrasts under shared-cohort locks. The companion cumulative-risk grammar covers time-to-event risks with censoring and competing risks, but the staged support-and-ladder machinery has not yet been extended to those estimands. Counterfactual hazard ratios, longitudinal treatments, and cumulative-count estimands sit outside the current scope; analysts who need them have survtmle (Benkeser and Hejazi 2018) and lmtp (Williams and Dı́az 2021) as alternative implementations, and can feed their output through the same lock records.

13.6 Future extensions

The most consequential extensions, in priority order, are:

  1. Single-call FIORD alignment. Both FIORD stages are now implemented (select_candidate(rule = "fiord_two_stage") for the point estimator, and select_variance_method() with bootstrap_rd_variance() for the variance method; see also Mertens, Zhang, et al. (2024)). Folding the variance stage into a single run_* wrapper and caching the bootstrap would make full FIORD alignment a one-call default in place of two explicit steps.
  2. Operating-characteristic validation of the variance selector at scale, paired with the gate validation in Section 11, so the variance-method choice is itself shown to recover nominal coverage across a range of data-generating processes.
  3. Unmeasured-confounding severity gradient: vary the strength of the latent-U scenario across a prespecified grid rather than running a single strong-U setting, so the DQ stress test produces an E-value-style sensitivity curve as a by-product.
  4. Pre-protocol stress-test mode: allow the plasmode and DQ stress test to run on user-specified covariate distributions and treatment-mechanism strength (no real data required) so that investigators can decide which dataset to use before any data-use agreement is signed.
  5. DGP-spectrum argument for the plasmode generator: structural- equation (simcausal-style), hybrid (current default), and parametric-bootstrap modes, with simulated-data fidelity metrics (Hellinger / Wasserstein, or covariate SMDs between real and simulated samples) so the analyst can judge whether the DGP is faithful enough to base candidate selection on.
  6. Matched-cohort vs full-cohort plasmode diagnostic: under a known simulated truth, compare the two estimators side by side to diagnose whether observed real-data gaps are sampling noise or positivity-driven.
  7. Richer simulated-outcome models: effect modification, time- varying treatment, and competing risks (the current DGP is a logistic regression with a constant additive effect on the risk-difference scale).
  8. MAR / MNAR missingness handling: the data-quality stress test now degrades covariates under MAR and MNAR, but the only handling it exercises is median imputation; a native inverse-probability-of- missingness or multiple-imputation path that does not require a structural missingness model remains future work.
  9. Survival and competing-risk estimands: wrapping survtmle (Benkeser and Hejazi 2018) and lmtp (Williams and Dı́az 2021) (and ltmle for the longitudinal FIORD setting) inside the lock and design-log machinery so that hazard-ratio and cumulative- incidence estimands inherit the same governance.
  10. Transportability and decision-population shift: the plasmode framework can in principle simulate covariate- distribution shift between the analytic cohort and the target population, but the package does not yet expose this scenario.
  11. Calibration helpers for severity ranges: small helpers that read validation-literature parameters (PPV, sensitivity, claims- accuracy ranges) from a YAML file and translate them into threats lists for stress_test(), with the citations attached to the design log.

13.7 When to use cleanTMLE inside a broader governance arrangement

For exploratory or lower-stakes RWE studies, cleanTMLE used on its own may be adequate to document and audit outcome-blind estimator selection: the analyst prespecifies the analytic plan, runs the workflow inside a single R session, and archives the analysis lock together with the exported design log. For high-stakes regulatory or confirmatory studies (FDA, EMA, or HTA submission contexts), cleanTMLE should be embedded within personnel-based outcome-blinding and access-control arrangements. That deployment places cleanTMLE inside a broader governed process with separate study-level work items: source-data audit and provenance, exposure and outcome phenotype validation, role-separated analyst and reviewer access, and an independent review of the pre-outcome decision by personnel who did not author the analytic plan. The software-mediated workflow records that the prespecified contract has been followed; the governed process establishes that the contract is the right one (Muntner et al. 2024; U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018; European Medicines Agency 2024).

13.8 Recommendations for practice

A fillable SAP template aligned with the prespecification checklist of Gruber, Lee, et al. (2024) and the staging construct of Muntner et al. (2024) is shipped with the package as system.file("templates", "sap_template.qmd", package = "cleanTMLE"). The template walks the analyst through the eight-section structure (estimand under ICH E9(R1), identifiability assumptions and DQ mappings, candidate grid, decision thresholds, NC domain coverage, sensitivity plan, decision log, reporting checklist) so that the prespecification is filed in the same form that the design log will later reference.

We recommend a five-step pre-outcome workflow when the analyst is preparing a TL-RWE study.

  1. Document the SPIFD2 template, citing validation studies or data profiling for each plausible range.
  2. Lock the specification and declare the estimand ladder: the primary estimand, the ordered fallbacks, the switching trigger, and the decision thresholds, all before any simulation runs.
  3. Fit the propensity and read the design: assess_support(), estimand_feasibility(), and simulate_support(). If the declared primary is unsupported, the ladder, not the analyst’s discretion, chooses what replaces it.
  4. Run stress_test() on the surviving estimand, first with no threats and then with the SPIFD2-derived ranges declared as threats, and lock the candidate with select_candidate().
  5. Assemble design_report() and score the pre-outcome decision. If a candidate is robust to the SPIFD2 plausible ranges, lock it. If no candidate is robust, the correct decision is to stop, and the analyst should reconsider the data source, the estimand, or the decision thresholds before unblinding.

The design log preserves all of the above. The final paper or regulatory submission can be reconstructed from the lock and the log, including the SPIFD2 ranges, the support and feasibility verdicts, the plasmode and DQ stress metrics, the pre-outcome decision, and the post-outcome estimates with any ladder switch.

14 Summary

cleanTMLE is an R package for staged, outcome-blind targeted learning that makes estimability a design-stage question and produces reproducible prespecification records. A traditional clean room establishes that the analyst did not peek; cleanTMLE additionally establishes whether the promised comparison was answerable, names the neighbouring estimand the data can support when it is not, and estimates that estimand with a doubly robust estimator, all committed before anyone saw an outcome. The support assessment, the per-estimand feasibility reading, the outcome-blind support map (built on the generate-treatment plasmode design of Shaw et al. (2025)), and the pre-registered estimand ladder implement the estimability half. The data-quality stress test implements the robustness half: it extends the outcome-blind plasmode loop of Dang et al. (2023) and Gruber, Lee, et al. (2024) with five data-quality degradation mechanisms, producing per-candidate degradation gradients on the same bias, RMSE, and coverage scale as the baseline plasmode so the prespecified decision rule applies uniformly to both, and a constructed demonstration (Section 10.4) shows the worst-case rule can lock a different candidate from the baseline rule. The package does not itself determine whether a data source is fit for purpose; the severity ranges entered into the stress test must come from prior validation studies, data profiling, or expert elicitation, and the support machinery reads only the measured covariates. The analysis-lock object and design log persist the prespecification as reproducible records. The package is available at https://github.com/amertens/cleanTMLE; the simulation code for the results in Section 10 is in the companion repository https://github.com/amertens/clean-room-sim.

15 Reproducibility

The cleanTMLE package ships 28 testthat test files covering the core workflow: analysis-lock creation and validation, the support assessment and per-estimand feasibility functions, the estimand ladder and its estimators (including recovery of known ATT and ATO truths and the Shaw-artifact design comparison), the DQ stress-test mechanics and degradation gradients, bootstrap and influence-function variance estimators (including the "match_tmle" estimator), event-process helpers, plasmode simulation, estimator ground-truth comparisons against tmle::tmle(), and reporting tables. Tests are run on every push through the repository’s continuous-integration configuration (cleanTMLE/tests/testthat/). The experimental time-to-event estimators have separate test files and are tagged accordingly.

15.1 Estimator validation against a reference implementation

In addition to the unit tests, we validate the package’s targeted-learning estimator against the reference tmle package on a single large sample (\(n = 20{,}000\)) from the Scenario A data-generating process, where the analytic marginal risk difference is known. The results show the cleanTMLE TMLE and tmle::tmle() agreeing to roughly four decimal places (a difference near \(0.0002\) in the risk difference, with near-identical standard errors), and both recovering the analytic truth (Table 13). This establishes that the estimator machinery is a correct implementation; the package’s distinct contributions are the staged outcome-blind governance and the data-quality stress test layered on top of a standard, validated estimator.

The simulation results reported in this paper are produced by the scripts listed below in the companion repository (https://github.com/amertens/clean-room-sim). Each writes to a tracked results directory: results_new/ for the main simulation and the variance study, rescueCo/results/ for the case study, and sandbox/ for the divergence and validation studies. Replicate counts, sample size, and output directory for the main simulation are set with the SIM_REPS, SIM_NOBS, and SIM_RESULTS environment variables (see RUN_MANIFEST.md).

We thank the targeted-learning RWE roadmap authors (Dang, Gruber, Phillips, Lee, Ho, van der Laan, Petersen, and colleagues), whose published frameworks this software builds on, and the broader cumulative-risk pharmacoepidemiology literature whose estimand framing motivated several of our diagnostic helpers. Any errors are ours.
